en: Preface to the Eleventh Assembly of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra: The Section on the Perfection of Giving (Dānapāramitā),
compiled by the Śramaṇa Xuánzé of Xīmíng Monastery.
Thus, while myriad virtues reflect one another, they are unified by the Three Bodies;
while myriad practices support one another, they are encompassed by the Six Perfections.
These are like the six feathers of a soaring bird or the six sensory faculties that await the dust of objects.
Therefore, in each separate assembly, these matters are individually elucidated according to their respective categories.
As for the foundation of benefiting sentient beings and the gradual process of relinquishing attachment, when one examines their essentials, none surpasses the practice of giving.

Yet, while giving alone may lead to sinking or rising, it truly relies upon guidance and analysis; thus, Śrāvastī was gathered again and Dāna was first proclaimed. This was intended so that the "three firmnesses" would not lose their guard and the "ten perfections" would become a ford. One should then tread the path of the four vows, unlock the secret pivot of the seven emptinesses, trample over the two vehicles to ascend directly, and shatter the three wheels to gallop afar.
When scrutinized through the lens of consciousness-only, what nation or city can be relied upon?
When dismissed as mere provisional names, how could head or eyes be considered the self?
When extended through sympathetic joy, merit flourishes spontaneously without being planted.
When it is bound together by dedication, it spreads spontaneously without being exhorted;
when it is guided by Bodhi, it reaches its goal spontaneously without being transferred;
when it is applied through skillful means, it merges spontaneously without being consciously thought of.
Therefore, one does not worry about the scarcity of things, but rather about the lack of magnanimity in one's mind;
one does not worry about the difficulty of giving, but rather about the ease with which one forgets to take back what was received.
To regard a solemn mind as purity is not yet to have reached its true solemnity;
to take the inclination toward stillness as truth is not yet to have realized its true stillness.

How much more so, then, regarding the pursuit of fame, reputation, fortune, and pleasure, or the anxieties concerning kings, thieves, water, and fire—how far removed these are from attaining the ultimate!
Thus, as for the destination of the great vows of the Greatly Awakened Ones: their giving of material wealth fulfills all categories of beings;
their giving of the Dharma exhausts all conscious creatures by leading them to liberation.
Thereafter, one forgets the means by which one acts and loses the basis for what is beneficial, until finally there is no further stimulus!
How magnificent is this accomplishment!

Only when this culture is truly spread can this aspiration be further expanded. Although Lu Jiuzhi’s nature was unshakeable and Bo Shang found it difficult to borrow [virtue], I still hope that through the gradual influence of your compassionate voice and the transformation of my own base parsimony, I may return from this state—then who could remain unchanged!
Its phrasing is abundant and its exhortations are profound and clear; it comprises five volumes in total and is not a re-translation.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree, Part One of the Eleventh Chapter on the Perfection of Giving (*Dānapāramitā*). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Bhagavat was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of one thousand three hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:
"When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of giving, how long must they pass before it is brought to fulfillment?"
Then, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The unsurpassed True Dharma has the Buddha as its root, the Buddha as its leader, and the Buddha as its foundation.”
“I only pray that the Blessed One will proclaim and reveal it, so that the assembly of bhikṣus, having heard it, may receive and uphold it!
At that time, the Blessed One exhorted Śāriputra a second and a third time, saying:
“You should now proclaim the perfection of generosity for the sake of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas.”

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, having been urged and exhorted by the Buddha with repeated and earnest entreaty, and sustained by the Buddha’s spiritual power, first instructed and taught the bodhisattva mahāsattvas regarding the perfection of generosity, saying:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, they should take omniscience as their objective support and, with great compassion as their foremost guide, practice the perfection of generosity."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva takes all-knowledge as their object and practices the perfection of generosity with great compassion as the foremost guide, that bodhisattva mahāsattva will be able to embrace all-knowledge and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas would rather practice giving with an indeterminate mind—or perhaps not practice giving at all—than ever practice giving with a mind that dedicates the merit toward the stages of the two vehicles.
"Why is this? Because all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should fear the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked Śāriputra:
“For what cause and for what reason should bodhisattva-mahāsattvas fear the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?
Śāriputra replied, “It is not that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas consider omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) to be equal to that of the two vehicles; rather, it is for this reason that I cause them to feel fear.”
Then, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra again asked the Venerable Śāriputra:
“What is the difference between the giving of bodhisattvas and the giving of śrāvakas? Śāriputra replied:
“Śrāvakas practice giving and dedicate it toward nirvāṇa and the fruit of arhatship; bodhisattvas practice giving and dedicate it toward bodhi and the knowledge of all modes—this is the distinction.”
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Suppose there are two people who both practice giving.
One seeks a superior fruit by taking the royal throne as his object; when he practices giving, he forms this thought: "
"May I, by virtue of this, become a great king who rules over the eight directions with complete sovereignty.
Following this aspiration, he later became a king, transforming the world through righteous governance and establishing it in sovereign peace and happiness.
First, there is one who seeks a superior fruit by taking the position of a minister as their object; when practicing generosity, they form this thought:
"May I, by means of this, become a great minister, beloved and entrusted by the king, and commissioned with authority to carry out whatever the king desires."
"By virtue of this vow, he ultimately did not become a king.
Although these two individuals both practiced giving, the results differed in quality according to their respective vows.

It is the same for Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas when practicing generosity: when Bodhisattvas practice giving, they take omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*) as their object, with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) as their primary motivation, and dedicate the merit of their practice toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) together with all sentient beings; by means of this, they are able to attain omniscience."
When the assembly of śrāvakas practices giving, they take the fruit of the śrāvaka as their object and seek their own liberation, not seeking unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Although both bodhisattvas and śrāvakas practice giving, there is a distinction between the excellence and inferiority of the fruits according to their respective aspirations: one attains the wisdom of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*) by virtue of giving, while the other attains the fruit of a śrāvaka by virtue of giving; this is what is meant by their difference.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
It is like a person who practices giving with the aim of becoming a head of a guild or a householder.

Then there is another person who practices giving, wishing to become a servant to those headmen or householders. You should know that the superiority and inferiority of the aspirations of Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas when practicing giving are likewise so."
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra praised Śāriputra, saying:
"The parable you have spoken is truly rare!
You have skillfully elucidated the distinction between the two kinds of giving; I, too, shall speak a parable regarding these two kinds of giving."
It is as if there were someone who, taking hundreds of thousands of jewels, went to a person of great wealth and spoke these words:
"I now offer these items to you, O Benevolent One; I pray that you will accept me and take me as a close servant, for I am capable of performing all tasks."
"The same applies to the śrāvakas who practice giving; they vow to become close disciples of the Tathāgata, whereas the bodhisattvas do not do so—this is what constitutes the distinction.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

Suppose there were a woman who, having abandoned the pleasures of the royal palace, took hundreds of thousands of jewels and went in secret to the house of a householder or a merchant chief, saying to him:
"I now offer these jewels; I pray you will accept me as your wife, and I shall serve you for the rest of my life without ever failing."
"In this way, the śrāvakas practice giving merely desiring to become disciples of the Tathāgata; the bodhisattvas are not so. This is what is meant by their distinction.
At that time, Śāriputra praised the venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, saying:
"Your skillful exposition of the parables of these two types of giving is truly rare!"
This means that the śrāvakas, lacking skillful means, practice giving with the aim of attaining the fruit of a śrāvaka;
whereas the bodhisattvas, possessing skillful means, practice giving for the sake of universally gathering and sustaining all sentient beings, thereby attaining omniscience.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should first practice generosity among all forms of conduct, forming this thought:

'I now perform this act of giving and bestow it upon all sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions, so that they may be forever liberated from the birth and death of the evil realms; and those who have not yet resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, may they quickly resolve their minds to do so.'"
For those who have already resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, may they never fall back;
for those who have already become non-retrogressive regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may they swiftly fulfill the knowledge of all modes of knowing.
"In this way, the bodhisattva contemplates that external objects are not separate from the internal mind, gathering all roots of goodness so that they gradually increase.

Whenever these bodhisattvas gather and protect the roots of goodness so that they do not decline, at those times they draw progressively closer to the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna). Whenever these bodhisattvas gradually draw closer to the knowledge of all modes, at those times their roots of goodness become perfected, and they proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, able to bring benefit and happiness to all beings throughout the future."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice generosity, they form this thought:
'May all sentient beings within the range of vision of my eyes obtain all such food, drink, and other things as I have bestowed and relinquished.'"
If sentient beings receive from me gifts such as food and drink, they may consume a small portion according to their own needs and then take the remainder to give it in turn to other sentient beings.
Those sentient beings enjoy a small portion of it and, in turn, hold and bestow it upon other sentient beings.
In this manner, through successive transmission, all within the realm of sentient beings equally enjoy the objects I have given.
By means of such causes and conditions of giving, I have gathered roots of goodness that are immeasurable and boundless.

Furthermore, taking these immeasurable roots of goodness, I bestow them universally upon all classes of sentient beings throughout the ten directions: may they all be forever liberated from the birth and death of the evil realms; may those who have not yet resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta quickly resolve to do so;
and may those who have already resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta never again fall back.
"If they have already become non-retrogressive regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, cause them to swiftly fulfill the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

Whenever these bodhisattvas gather and successively increase their roots of virtue, at those times these bodhisattvas gather all the perfections (pāramitās). Whenever these bodhisattvas gather all the perfections, at those times these bodhisattvas draw progressively closer to the knowledge of all modes.

One should know that these bodhisattvas, through their skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), obtain immeasurable roots of goodness from the act of giving, even when bestowing but a small amount. Why is this?
“Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Because the mind of giving is without limit or boundary, it is dedicated toward the realization of all-knowledge.
Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!”
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice generosity, they give rise to this thought:

"May the roots of goodness from my giving not bring about any other fruit, but rather may I realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, so as to bring benefit and happiness to all beings throughout the future."

When such dedication is directed toward unsurpassed enlightenment and not toward any other result, it is called the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), causing all perfections to be fully accomplished.

If one lacks the final thought that dedicates all-knowledge toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, then although one practices generosity, it is not the perfection of generosity; nor can it cause the other perfections one has cultivated to be swiftly fulfilled, nor can one attain the knowledge of all modes of knowledge.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

Although the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas may give only a small amount of alms, if they can dedicate it toward unexcelled bodhi, you should know that the measure of their giving is profound and vast, for they will certainly be able to realize all-knowledge."

Although bodhisattva-mahāsattvas may practice extensive giving, if they do not dedicate it toward unsurpassed enlightenment, you should know that such giving is limited and narrow in scope, as it cannot lead to the realization of all-knowledge.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices generosity but does not give rise to the subsequent thought of dedicating it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, nor takes all-knowledge as an object, then although this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices generosity, it is not the perfection of generosity; it can only produce birth and death, not all-knowledge."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing generosity, is able to give rise to a subsequent thought that dedicates it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and furthermore takes omniscience as its object, then the generosity practiced by this bodhisattva mahāsattva is called the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*); it does not produce rebirth in saṃsāra, but leads to the attainment of omniscience.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices generosity without attachment, dedicates it toward unsurpassed enlightenment without attachment, and focuses upon the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñājñāna) without attachment—this bodhisattva mahāsattva, through skillful means, swiftly brings the perfection of generosity to completion, causes all the perfections to reach ultimate fulfillment, quickly realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and is able to bring benefit and happiness to all beings throughout the future."
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked Śāriputra:
"Regarding this essential teaching spoken by the Venerable One, is it from your own eloquence, or do you rely upon the power of the Buddha?"
Śāriputra said: "I have spoken this essential teaching by relying on the power of the Buddha; it is not through my own eloquence.
Then, Śāriputra further addressed the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, saying:

"Suppose all sentient beings in the infinite, countless, and boundless worlds of the ten directions, desiring to realize the fruit of Arhatship, were for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River to give away various material goods—whether to countless ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), or to countless Śrāvakas, or to countless Pratyekabuddhas—the merit they would thereby obtain would be immeasurable, incalculable, and inconceivable."
There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, taking that generosity as their object, form this thought:
"I rejoice in all the accumulations of merit obtained by those sentient beings."

This bodhisattva mahāsattva further takes all these roots of goodness—consisting of all such meritorious deeds accompanied by sympathetic joy—and universally bestows them upon all sentient beings throughout the ten directions. He makes this vow: "May they all be forever liberated from the birth and death of the evil realms. May those who have not yet resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta quickly resolve to do so;
may those who have already resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta never again fall back;
and may those who have already reached the stage of non-retrogression regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment quickly fulfill the knowledge of all modes."
By means of these roots of goodness dedicated through sympathetic joy, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring to full completion the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

All the roots of goodness dedicated through sympathetic joy possessed by this bodhisattva mahāsattva surpass the mass of merit from the previous beings' acts of giving a hundredfold, a thousandfold, and even up to an *upaniṣad*-fold more.

In this way, the mind of a bodhisattva that rejoices and dedicates surpasses the merit of the giving practiced by all sentient beings in the world; this is the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of a bodhisattva, whereby even with little exertion, the merit is immeasurable.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

Suppose all sentient beings in the infinite, incalculable, and boundless worlds of the ten directions were to dwell for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, constantly offering immeasurable and boundless articles of worship to the Buddhas and the community of bhikṣus; by reason of this, they would obtain immeasurable merit."
There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, with a profound mind, rejoice in that mass of merit, thinking:

"How excellent! Those sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions who are able to reverently make offerings to such a truly pure field of merit, their bodies and minds never wearying."
"Excellent! I deeply rejoice in that merit.

The mass of merit produced by this bodhisattva mahāsattva through such a mind of sympathetic joy surpasses, by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, and even up to an *upaniṣad*-fold, all the merit from the offerings made to the Buddha and the Saṅgha by all sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
In this way, the mind of sympathetic joy of a bodhisattva surpasses the merit of all worldly acts of giving.

Just as the light of all the jewels, fire-crystals, and other luminous objects within the four continents, though capable of shining, is entirely eclipsed by the radiance emitted by the lunar disc; so too, although the merit from the acts of giving performed by all sentient beings throughout the ten directions is immeasurable, it is eclipsed by the roots of virtue induced by the bodhisattva’s mind of sympathetic joy.

Just as all the light existing within the realms of the four continents is eclipsed by the radiance of the sun, so too are all the merits from the acts of giving performed by sentient beings throughout the ten directions eclipsed by the roots of goodness arising from a bodhisattva’s sympathetic joy.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

It is as if a great multitude of hundreds of thousands of *kañcana* mani-jewels were gathered in one place; although they possess various mixed-colored radiances, if someone were to take a single *vaiḍūrya* jewel and place it atop that heap, all those various colored radiances would be completely eclipsed."

Thus, even if all sentient beings throughout the ten directions were to remain for immeasurable *gaṅgā*-sands of eons, constantly bestowing various kinds of supreme and exquisite objects of enjoyment upon other sentient beings, or upon the Buddha and the Saṃgha, the merit obtained by a single Bodhisattva who gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) toward that mass of merit would surpass that mass of merit by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, and even up to an *upaniṣad*-fold.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

Suppose hundreds of thousands of ordinary worldly horses were gathered in one place; if the horse-treasure of a Wheel-turning King were to enter among them, it would cause all of their splendor to vanish."

Thus, although all sentient beings in the ten directions were to dwell for immeasurable *gaṅgā*-sands of eons, practicing generosity and accumulating roots of virtue, the merit obtained by a single bodhisattva through rejoicing (*anumodanā*) with a profound mind in those roots of virtue would surpass those roots of virtue by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, and even up to an *upaniṣad*-fold.

"In this way, the mind of sympathetic joy possessed by a bodhisattva outshines the meritorious deeds of worldly giving; therefore, a bodhisattva who wishes to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should deeply rejoice in the merits performed by all sentient beings."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should take the various meritorious deeds associated with the mind of sympathetic joy they have generated and bestow them upon all sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions. They should make this vow: 'May all these sentient beings of the ten directions be forever liberated from the saṃsāra of the evil realms; may those who have not yet resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta quickly resolve to do so;
and may those who have already resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta never again fall back.'"
If they have already become non-retrogressive regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they shall swiftly fulfill the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).
Whenever these bodhisattvas relinquish their roots of goodness to sentient beings, at those very times these bodhisattvas draw ever closer to the knowledge of all modes.

Whenever these bodhisattvas do not grasp at their own roots of goodness as "mine," at those very times these bodhisattvas are able to dedicate those roots of goodness to sentient beings, vowing that all may be free from suffering and attain eternal peace and happiness.

Whenever these bodhisattvas relinquish their own roots of virtue to bestow upon sentient beings, at those times, even though they do not cultivate the provisions for enlightenment (*bodhi-sambhāra*), they are able to draw near to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).

Whenever these bodhisattvas do not grasp at their own roots of virtue as "mine," but give them to all sentient beings throughout the ten directions, vowing that they all be free from suffering and attain eternal peace and happiness, at those times the roots of virtue of these bodhisattvas increase and advance; they draw near to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) and are able to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes.
Whenever these bodhisattvas do not grasp at their own roots of virtue as "mine," at those times these bodhisattvas gather and sustain immeasurable, preeminent roots of virtue.
Why is this? Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Because the mental state of this bodhisattva is without limitation, as he dedicates [his merit] toward the realization of all-knowledge (sarvajñatā).

"In this way, through the skillful means of a mind accompanied by sympathetic joy, although the bodhisattva takes up the roots of virtue induced by that sympathetic joy and dedicates them for the sake of sentient beings, they have no attachment whatsoever to those roots of virtue or to the class of sentient beings;

although they vow to liberate sentient beings from the miseries of the evil destinies and from birth-and-death, they have no attachment whatsoever to those evil destinies or to the sufferings of birth-and-death;
although they vow to gather in all classes of sentient beings and cause them to resolve upon unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they have no attachment whatsoever to that resolution."
Although he vows to gather in all classes of sentient beings so that they may never regress from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, he has no attachment whatsoever to this state;

although he vows to gather in all classes of sentient beings so that their bodhisattva practices may quickly reach fulfillment and they may swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes, he has no attachment whatsoever to this state;
and although he vows to personally attain the knowledge of all modes, he likewise has no attachment to this knowledge.
Thus, when a bodhisattva is free from any grasping view, one should know that this constitutes skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*).

Because all such minds of a bodhisattva—conjoined with sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) and dedication (*pariṇāmanā*)—possess the power of skill in means, they are able to universally sustain the assembly of other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, causing them to obtain supreme benefit and happiness, while also personally embracing the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*) and swiftly realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

Suppose all sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions were to dwell for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, constantly offering various kinds of supreme and exquisite requisites to the Buddhas and the community of bhikṣus, making offerings, showing reverence, honoring, and praising them while cultivating various meritorious deeds."

If there were a bodhisattva who, holding a single bowl of food, offered it to the Buddha and the Sangha, the merit thereof would surpass that [previous merit] by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, and even up to an *upaniṣad*-fold.

Why is this? It is because this bodhisattva does not perceive a giver, does not perceive a recipient, and does not perceive the gift. Although they contemplate that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty, when practicing generosity, they never depart from dedication and aspiration; that is, they take the merit of the gift and, together with sentient beings, dedicate it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, vowing to realize the wisdom of all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna) together with them.

Therefore, when a bodhisattva practices generosity, the merit they generate through giving to sentient beings is a hundred times superior, a thousand times superior, and even up to an *upaniṣad*-fold (infinitely) superior; by means of this, they will certainly realize unsurpassed enlightenment and bring benefit, peace, and happiness to all classes of sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of generosity, they should give rise to this thought:

'I now bestow and relinquish such wealth and goods; whatever superior roots of goodness are thereby produced, I universally offer them to all sentient beings throughout the ten directions: may those who are in the hells quickly emerge from hell;'"
May those dwelling among animals be swiftly liberated from the animal realm;
may those residing in the realm of hungry ghosts be swiftly freed from the ghost realm;
and for all those in the human and celestial realms who experience sorrow and suffering, may all their sorrow and suffering be forever stilled.
May those who weary of birth and death swiftly emerge from the three realms;
may those infinite and boundless sentient beings throughout the ten directions who have not yet resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta quickly give rise to that resolve;
and may those who have already resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta never again fall back.
"If they have already become non-retrogressive regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I shall cause them to swiftly fulfill the knowledge of all aspects.
Whenever these bodhisattvas relinquish their roots of virtue to sentient beings, at those times these bodhisattvas embrace the perfection of generosity;
whenever these bodhisattvas embrace the perfection of generosity, at those times these bodhisattvas increase all the perfections.
Whenever these bodhisattvas increase all the pāramitās, at those times they gather immeasurable and preeminent roots of virtue;
whenever these bodhisattvas gather immeasurable and preeminent roots of virtue, at those times they progressively draw near to the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
Thus, through skillful means, a bodhisattva attains great merit even with little effort.
Therefore, a bodhisattva who wishes to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should always diligently cultivate skillful means.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Whenever these bodhisattvas do not grasp at their own roots of goodness as 'mine,' at those very times these bodhisattvas gather and receive immeasurable and boundless roots of goodness."
Why is this? It is because these bodhisattvas desire that immeasurable and boundless sentient beings may all swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

Such bodhisattvas are able to relinquish everything; they can even redirect and bestow their own roots of virtue upon other immeasurable and boundless sentient beings—how much more so, then, could they not relinquish their own roots of virtue!
If they are still able to generously relinquish all their roots of virtue, how much more so other precious wealth!

Thus, such a bodhisattva is able to relinquish all material and immaterial things, able to relinquish all superior roots of virtue belonging to both self and others, and even able to relinquish the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), bestowing them upon all sentient beings so that they may likewise realize it.
Thus the Bodhisattva makes this great lion’s roar:

"I do not perceive anything at all among all phenomena; I do not perceive any internal or external objects, whether material or immaterial. Although I perceive nothing, I am able to relinquish everything."
Thus, the bodhisattva reflects:
"I do not see any phenomenon or any object that I am unable to relinquish as a gift to sentient beings.
When such a bodhisattva realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they observe the world with the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*) and let out a great lion's roar:

"I see nothing at all in any phenomena; I see nothing among any internal or external things, whether they possess form or are formless. Although I see nothing, I am able to relinquish everything; that is to say, I do not see any phenomenon or any object such that I would be unable to give it to sentient beings."
Thus, a bodhisattva constantly reflects:
"When I have realized unsurpassed awakening, I shall see nothing at all regarding any phenomena; yet, while seeing nothing, there shall be no phenomenon that I do not directly realize or fully know."
Because Bodhisattvas are able to relinquish everything, when they realize unsurpassed enlightenment, they are able to relinquish all phenomena to the ultimate degree;
through this ultimate relinquishment, there is no phenomenon that they do not directly realize and no phenomenon that they do not fully know.
To the extent that one does not fail to relinquish any phenomenon, to that same extent one perceives no phenomenon at all;
to the extent that one perceives no phenomenon at all, to that same extent one realizes all phenomena without exception and knows them all without exception.

In this way, a bodhisattva is able to relinquish both the internal and the external; because they are able to relinquish all phenomena, both internal and external, they perceive nothing at all. Because they perceive nothing regarding all phenomena, when they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, there is no phenomenon that they do not directly realize or fully know, and they are thus able to bring benefit and happiness to all beings throughout the future.
“Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

All bodhisattvas should train in this way in the pure perfection of giving. If bodhisattvas can train in this way in the pure perfection of giving, they are called true and pure bodhisattvas, and they never depart from the mind of omniscience.”

When a bodhisattva is never separated from the mind of omniscience, at that time even all the evil Māras cannot find an opportunity, let alone other yakṣas, piśācas, and the like who might gain an advantage!
It is impossible that any sentient beings could gain an advantage over such bodhisattvas.

Why is this? Because in whatever place bodhisattvas practice the perfection of generosity, never for a moment ceasing to direct their minds toward omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*), neither humans nor non-humans can find an opportunity there.
Why is this? Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If one constantly contemplates the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), such mental attention is inconceivable, vast, profound, and rare in the world, because the knowledge of all modes is inconceivable, vast, profound, and difficult to fathom.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If bodhisattvas can train in this way in the practice of great enlightenment, they possess great beneficence toward all sentient beings and are able to properly nurture all sentient beings; that is to say, they cause the various classes of sentient beings in the world to be free from calamities, to abandon evil, and to cultivate goodness."
For this reason, while Bodhisattvas abide in the stage of a bodhisattva, they are constantly able to bring benefit and happiness to all ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.

Furthermore, when these bodhisattvas realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they likewise possess great merit and virtue toward sentient beings, being able to skillfully nurture all sentient beings. That is to say, by teaching the true Dharma so that afflictions may be severed, they enable immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to attain nirvāṇa and ultimate peace and happiness.

"Therefore, when a bodhisattva realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they become the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the most exalted, the most sublime, the most wondrous, the highest, and the unsurpassed among all ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas—peerless and equal to the unequaled."

Even after his parinirvāṇa, he likewise possesses great beneficence toward sentient beings, for he is able to skillfully nurture all sentient beings. This means that by making offerings, paying homage, showing respect, and offering praise at the stūpas of the Tathāgata—presenting various kinds of exquisite flower garlands, powdered and scattered incenses, robes, necklaces, jeweled banners, flags, canopies, music, and lamps—sentient beings plant immeasurable and supreme roots of virtue through these causes and conditions. Alternatively, having heard the essential teachings on the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa, they diligently practice and train until they realize parinirvāṇa.

Even those who offer as little as a single incense stick or a single flower at the stūpas of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One records that they shall all become free from desire, and many will ultimately attain parinirvāṇa.
In this way, when a bodhisattva abides in the bodhisattva stage, they possess great benevolence toward all sentient beings and are able to properly nurture all sentient beings.
When they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, they likewise possess great benevolence toward sentient beings and are able to properly nurture all sentient beings.
Even after their parinirvāṇa, they likewise possess great merit and virtue toward sentient beings, for they are able to skillfully nurture all sentient beings.

Because Bodhisattvas always possess great merit and virtue toward sentient beings and are able to skillfully nurture all sentient beings, they are the most honored and supreme in the world; none can equal them except for the Buddhas.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
If bodhisattvas accomplish such sublime merits, these bodhisattvas constantly bring great benefit to sentient beings."

For example, just as genuine gold can always benefit all sentient beings—whether it has been smelted or not, whether it has been fashioned into ornaments or not, and whether it has been refined or not—it is always able to benefit all sentient beings.

In this way, when a bodhisattva cultivates the practices for awakening, abides in the bodhisattva stage, they are able to bring great benefit to sentient beings; when they realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they likewise bring great benefit to sentient beings; and even after their parinirvāṇa, they continue to bring great benefit to sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

Just as the orbs of the sun and moon traverse the four continents, bringing great benefit to all sentient beings—meaning that all sentient beings within the four continents perform their various activities through the illumination and touch of the light of the sun and moon, and are further able to discern the differences between day and night, the half-month and the full moon, as well as the seasons and years."
Furthermore, just as all flowers, fruits, crops, grasses, and trees, by being illuminated by the light of the sun and moon, grow, ripen, and nourish sentient beings;

so too does a bodhisattva who cultivates the practices for enlightenment and dwells in the bodhisattva stage bring great benefit to sentient beings. When they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, they likewise bring great benefit to sentient beings, and even after their parinirvāṇa, they continue to bring great benefit to sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
These bodhisattvas, having accomplished such vast merit, constantly bring great benefit to sentient beings.

It is like a caravan leader who possesses abundant treasures and is able to provide all the necessities of life for hundreds of thousands of merchant companions and their kin, so that even after his death, those sentient beings continue to enjoy abundance and happiness through his wealth."

If a bodhisattva practicing the conduct of awakening and abiding in the stage of a bodhisattva can still bring benefit and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings, how much more so after attaining awakening and parinirvāṇa, when possessing great power, could they not cause their disciples and others to attain benefit, peace, and happiness?
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

Thus, a bodhisattva is always able to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings; that is to say, whether in the stage of a bodhisattva, upon attaining perfect enlightenment, or upon entering parinirvāṇa, they constantly perform great benefit for sentient beings, never abandoning them for even a moment."

Just as a virtuous person who possesses the marks of a virtuous person can bring peace and happiness to themselves and also bring peace and happiness to all other sentient beings, and who skillfully gathers precious wealth and skillfully distributes it, they are therefore called a "virtuous person" (*satpuruṣa*).

In this way, the bodhisattva, having well gathered various treasures of merit while in the stage of a bodhisattva, is well able to bring benefit and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings; when he realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, he likewise well brings benefit and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings; and even after his parinirvāṇa, he continues to well bring benefit and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings—meaning that even after nirvāṇa, the power of his merit continues to well bring benefit and happiness to his disciples and others.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

Whether in the stage of a bodhisattva, upon attaining bodhi, or after entering nirvāṇa, such a bodhisattva is always able to benefit and bring happiness to all sentient beings, never abandoning them for even a moment."

Just as those virtuous persons, endowed with the marks of a virtuous person, are able to bring peace and happiness to both themselves and others, and cause them to remain far removed from all manner of unfavorable circumstances; so too it is with the assembly of Bodhisattvas. They are able to cause both themselves and others to constantly attain peace and happiness, to remain far removed from all manner of evil karma and afflictions, and not fall into the cycle of birth and death within the miserable realms, but instead attain the ultimate peace and happiness of *parinirvāṇa*, or achieve perfect enlightenment to benefit all beings.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

Just as one born of the kṣatriya lineage who has received the consecration is worthy of succeeding to the royal throne—whether as a crown prince or when acting as king—he brings peace and happiness to all śramaṇas, brahmins, and other sentient beings."

Even after his life has ended, he is able to bring peace and happiness to the sentient beings of that land so that they suffer no decline or affliction; that is to say, by the residual power of that king’s merit, the land becomes prosperous and joyful, free from enemies, thieves, and the like.

In this way, when a bodhisattva practices the conduct of awakening, abides in the stage of a bodhisattva, they are already able to bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings; when they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, they are likewise able to bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings; and even after their parinirvāṇa, they are still able to bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings. That is to say, after their nirvāṇa, immeasurable sentient beings obtain immeasurable merit by making offerings, paying respect, honoring, and praising their stūpas; and they also attain boundless virtuous benefits by hearing the true Dharma, receiving and upholding it, reading and reciting it, reflecting upon it according to principle, and explaining it to others.

When sentient beings, after the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, recollect the Tathāgata’s aggregate of ethical discipline, aggregate of concentration, aggregate of wisdom, aggregate of liberation, and aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation, those sentient beings, by reason of this cause and condition, will not fall into the evil realms; they will be born among gods and humans where they constantly experience happiness, or some will realize the Nirvāṇa of the Three Vehicles, thereby enabling themselves and others to attain ultimate peace and bliss.
Those sentient beings, within their present bodies, cannot be harmed by humans or non-humans, nor can they be afflicted or disturbed by any matters of fear. Why is this?
"Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Recollecting the merits of the Buddha can extinguish the fears of humans and non-humans in the world.
At that time, the Buddha praised Śāriputra, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent! It is just as you have said.”

If there are classes of sentient beings who can recollect the Tathāgata’s aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of meditative concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation, those sentient beings will be able to extinguish all fears of humans, non-humans, and other such things in the world.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How extraordinary,
World-Honored One!"
“The Tathāgata has accomplished such pure, vast, and sublime dharmas.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:
“You should know that bodhisattvas also accomplish such pure, vast, and sublime dharmas.”
Śāriputra asked, “What is meant by the pure, vast, and sublime Dharma accomplished by a bodhisattva?
The Buddha replied:
“The pure, vast, and sublime Dharma accomplished by Bodhisattvas refers to the generation of the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment from which one never again regresses.
Why is this so, Śāriputra?
The most supremely pure, vast, and wondrous Dharma refers to the nature of the Tathāgata, the nature of spontaneous awakening, and the nature of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
If bodhisattvas have already resolved upon unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and do not regress, they will certainly achieve such pure, vast, and wondrous Dharma.
Then, Śāriputra again addressed the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, saying:
“The assembly of bodhisattvas should give rise to this thought:
‘If sentient beings come to me and seek various necessities of life;’”
I shall resolve to give with a mind of certain generosity; I must not give rise to a mind that lacks the necessary requisites.
Even if I currently possess no requisites to seek out, I must employ skillful means to find and give them; I shall never give rise to such a thought as:
"Since I currently have no requisites to seek out, I should not employ skillful means to find them for him."
If other sentient beings give to them of their own accord, I shall rejoice in it;
if they do not wish to give, I shall employ various skillful means to exhort and inspire them, so that the wishes of the seekers are fulfilled.

"In this way, whether a bodhisattva gives to sentient beings the requisites they require, or personally serves their teachers, elders, and the sick, all such meritorious deeds are shared equally with sentient beings and dedicated toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Desiring to benefit and bring happiness to all throughout the future, they seek to cause them to escape the miserable realms or the suffering of birth and death, and to attain nirvāṇa or omniscience."
If sentient beings practice giving themselves and cultivate other meritorious deeds, the bodhisattva encourages them to dedicate those merits toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The mass of merit thus obtained by the bodhisattva surpasses the merit from the giving of other sentient beings by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, and even by an *upaniṣad*-fold (infinitely).

Why is this? Because when a bodhisattva inspires and dedicates their mind, they are able to cause both themselves and all classes of sentient beings to together realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
When the assembly of bodhisattvas practices the perfection of generosity, they should first cultivate skillful means;
according to the skillful means they have cultivated, they practice generosity."

In accordance with whatever meritorious deeds of giving one practices, one dedicates them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, vowing that all sentient beings may likewise realize the wisdom of all-knowledge.
In this way, a bodhisattva’s skill in means enables both oneself and others to attain benefit.

If a bodhisattva practices generosity without first cultivating skill in means, even if they remain practicing generosity for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, they will be unable to resolve to dedicate that practice together with sentient beings toward enlightenment; they will be unable to fully embrace the perfection of generosity they have practiced; and they will be unable to realize the omniscience they originally sought.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Suppose there were sentient beings who, carrying vast vessels equal in measure to a trichiliocosm, went to where a bodhisattva was and said to that bodhisattva:
'We now require these vessels to be filled; we pray that you grant them quickly.'"
The Bodhisattva does not give rise to any other thought toward them, but gives rise only to this thought:
"I must certainly bestow [this gift].
That is to say, he never gives rise to a mind of anger or resentment.
"Thinking, 'This sentient being has treated me with slightness,' he likewise does not give rise to the thought of non-giving, saying:
'How could I bestow many things upon him?'"
Furthermore, they do not give rise to a mind of lacking wealth and treasures, thinking:
"How can I possibly procure such various kinds of wealth and treasures as to fill the vessels held by those sentient beings, which are equal in measure to a great trichiliocosm?"

He simply thinks: "I shall now cultivate supreme supernormal powers for their sake; by means of various skillful methods, I will gather all manner of wealth and treasures so that the wishes of those who seek them are surely fulfilled."

At that time, the Bodhisattva applies himself with fervent diligence and performs great exertion to seek superior supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), desiring to gather precious wealth to bestow upon those who come seeking; thus he embraces the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).

Having attained these supernormal powers, he gathers vast quantities of treasures and bestows them upon those who come seeking, fulfilling their wishes; thus he embraces the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*).
This is called the practice of the bodhisattvas’ perfection of generosity, in which they give rise to a vast mind that is ever free from weariness;
by means of this, they swiftly realize unsurpassed enlightenment and are able to bring benefit and happiness to all beings throughout the future.

"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice giving out of compassion for sentient beings; they should practice giving while abiding in a mind of loving-kindness to bestow happiness upon sentient beings; they should practice giving while abiding in a mind of compassion to extract suffering from sentient beings; they should practice giving while abiding in a mind of sympathetic joy to rejoice in sentient beings' departure from suffering and attainment of happiness; and they should practice giving while abiding in a mind of equanimity to benefit all classes of sentient beings impartially."
Having given in this manner, one should give rise to this thought:

"May the merit I have performed and the goodness I have cultivated be universally bestowed upon all sentient beings throughout the ten directions, so that they may forever be liberated from the evil realms and the cycle of birth and death; may those who have not yet resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta quickly resolve to do so;
and may those who have already resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta never again fall back."
"If they have already become non-retrogressive regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, cause them to swiftly fulfill the knowledge of all modes.
Whenever these bodhisattvas relinquish their roots of merit and virtue to sentient beings, at those very times, the roots of merit of these bodhisattvas increase.

Whenever these bodhisattvas dedicate the roots of goodness they have cultivated toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment for the sake of all sentient beings, vowing that they and others may together realize the knowledge of all modes, at those times their roots of goodness increase.
“Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
It is like pure gold: whenever it is smelted, refined, heated, and beaten, at those times its radiance and color become increasingly brilliant;
and whenever its radiance and color become increasingly brilliant, at those times it becomes progressively more malleable and fit for use as a vessel.”

In this way, whenever a bodhisattva dedicates the roots of virtue they have performed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, vowing that all sentient beings may likewise realize the knowledge of all modes, at those times their roots of virtue become increasingly flourishing;
and whenever their roots of virtue become increasingly flourishing, at those times they draw ever closer to the knowledge of all modes.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

It is like a woman polishing the surface of a mirror: whenever she applies effort to polish it, at that very time the mirror becomes increasingly bright and pure; and whenever the mirror becomes increasingly bright and pure, at that very time the various images appear upon the stainless surface of the mirror."

In this way, whenever a bodhisattva definitively dedicates their performed merit and performed virtue toward omniscient wisdom (*sarvajñajñāna*), at those very times they are able to universally bestow these upon all sentient beings in the worlds of the ten directions, causing them to be forever liberated from the birth and death of the evil realms; causing those who have not yet resolved for unsurpassed bodhicitta to swiftly resolve upon it;
causing those who have already resolved for unsurpassed bodhicitta never to regress;
and causing those who have already reached the stage of non-regression regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment to swiftly fulfill omniscient wisdom.
Whenever these bodhisattvas relinquish their own roots of virtue to bestow them upon sentient beings, at those very times their roots of virtue become increasingly flourishing;
and whenever their roots of virtue become increasingly flourishing, at those very times they draw ever closer to the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

In this way, through the bodhisattva’s skillful means, they dedicate [their merit] toward the sought-after knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), causing all virtues to increase gradually, swiftly realizing unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, and being able to benefit all beings throughout the future.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
How is it that a bodhisattva practices extensive giving yet acquires little merit?
And how is it that a bodhisattva practices limited giving yet acquires great merit?"
What is it for a bodhisattva to practice giving sparingly and thereby acquire little merit?
What is it for a bodhisattva to practice giving extensively and thereby acquire great merit?

If a bodhisattva, even after passing through as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, constantly relinquishes immeasurable and innumerable treasures and bestows them universally upon all sentient beings throughout the ten directions, yet does not dedicate this toward unsurpassed enlightenment—vowing instead that all sentient beings together realize the knowledge of all modes—such a bodhisattva practices giving extensively but acquires little merit.

If bodhisattvas, even for a brief duration, bestow a small amount of material wealth upon sentient beings and dedicate it toward unexcelled enlightenment, vowing that all sentient beings may together realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), such bodhisattvas gather vast merit through this minor practice of giving.

If a bodhisattva, for even a brief period, bestows a small amount of material wealth upon sentient beings but does not dedicate it toward unsurpassed enlightenment, wishing instead that all sentient beings together realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), such a bodhisattva performs only a minor act of giving and thereby acquires only a small measure of merit.

If bodhisattvas, throughout great eons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, constantly relinquish immeasurable and incalculable treasures and universally bestow them upon all sentient beings of the ten directions, and further dedicate these merits toward unsurpassed enlightenment, vowing that all sentient beings together realize the knowledge of all modes, such bodhisattvas practice extensive giving and thereby gather vast merit.

Therefore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should dedicate their roots of virtue together with all sentient beings toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, vowing that they and all sentient beings may together attain the knowledge of all modes.

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to be able to gather an immeasurable mass of merit, to bring great benefit to all sentient beings, and to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes, they should always remain inseparable from the mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all modes while practicing the perfection of generosity.”

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva never departs from the mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all aspects while practicing the perfection of generosity, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to gather an immeasurable mass of merit, swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and bring great benefit to all sentient beings.
Why is this so, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra?

If bodhisattvas constantly do not depart from the mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*) while practicing the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), the roots of virtue and merit of these bodhisattvas will gradually increase moment by moment. By means of this, they swiftly realize unsurpassed enlightenment and are able to bring benefit and happiness to all beings throughout the future.

Therefore, a bodhisattva who wishes to constantly bring about the welfare and happiness of sentient beings should always diligently cultivate skillful means among all practices, dedicating them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, and vowing to provide great benefit to sentient beings.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 579. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part Two of the Eleventh Section on the Perfection of Giving. "Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!"
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should, among all practices, first train in the perfection of unstained generosity.
Why is this? Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If one trains in the perfection of generosity, the stains of stinginess practiced since beginningless time are immediately distanced, and the continuity of body and mind gradually becomes able to draw near to the knowledge of all modes of being (*sarvajñajñāna*).

Therefore, whenever and at whatever time a bodhisattva maintains a continuous presence of mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), at those times and at those moments they gradually draw near to the knowledge of all modes;

whenever and at whatever time they gradually draw near to the knowledge of all modes, at those times and at those moments they gradually distance themselves from the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;

and whenever and at whatever time they gradually distance themselves from the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, at those times and at those moments they once again draw closer to the knowledge of all modes.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

It is like when it rains from heaven: if one places a jar in a place where water collects, it gradually fills up. When it is thus full, it is due to the continuous pouring of raindrops over a long period of time, not merely by the first or the last drop."

In this way, when a bodhisattva seeks omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), it is not attained through the initial arising of the mind alone, nor is it attained solely by the final arising of the mind while seated upon the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) at a later time; rather, from the initial mind continuing in succession until the final mind arises while seated upon the seat of enlightenment, they attain omniscience through their mutual support and progression.

In seeking omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), there is no initial, middle, or final moment of mind that cannot induce omniscience and lead to the realization of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*); for this is accomplished only through the successive continuity of these moments of mind, which suppress and sever the factors that constitute obstacles.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
If bodhisattvas wish to swiftly realize unsurpassed enlightenment, they should not allow their minds to be distracted or intermingled with other things.
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:
“What is meant by the state in which the minds of the bodhisattvas are free from intermixture? Śāriputra replied:
“If, when improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) manifests, bodhisattvas are able to correctly observe it as follows:”
"This accords with the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) and does not oppose it.
These bodhisattvas are able to know things as they truly are:

"The improper mental attention (ayoniśomanasikāra) that I have now aroused can serve as an aid to the knowledge of all modes; that is, the improper mental attention I have aroused can lead to the acquisition of a personal existence (ātmabhāva), causing me to remain long in the continuity of birth and death for the benefit of sentient beings."

If my own body were not sustained by the guidance of improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*), it would immediately perish; since I could not even bring my own practice to fulfillment, how could I possibly benefit other sentient beings?
"This much is called the state in which the minds of the bodhisattvas are free from intermixture.
Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If bodhisattvas are able to contemplate all phenomena—whether they be favorable or adverse—as being able to assist and lead toward the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), [they are thus established in this state]."

These bodhisattvas, through their skillful means, contemplate all phenomena such that they are able to accord with the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, without being interrupted by a mind of either attraction or aversion. They do not give rise to anger toward adverse objects, nor do they give rise to craving toward favorable objects; whether adverse or favorable, they are able to correctly know them as auxiliary conditions that lead to omniscience. Thus, at all times and regarding all objects, the minds of these bodhisattvas remain uninterrupted and unmixed.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
It is as if there were a person who, having been captured by others and led to the place of execution, was filled with such terror that he had no other thought in mind, but only this:
'Before long, I shall certainly be put to death by these others.'"

The assembly of bodhisattvas is likewise: if they constantly contemplate the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) and no other mental engagement arises in the interim, these bodhisattvas, at all times, will not be interspersed with other thoughts.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
It is as if there were a person who, carrying much precious wealth, entered a wilderness where many fierce and violent bandits dwelt;
at that time, that person would have no other thought, but would think only this:"
"When shall I emerge from such a place of peril and hardship, and reach a land of abundance, joy, peace, and security?

In the same way, when the assembly of bodhisattvas constantly contemplates the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), no other mental engagements can arise; these bodhisattvas possess purity of body and mind, untainted by any other thoughts.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

Suppose there is a person who has previously committed robbery and is being sought out by the king. In his terror, he secretly enters a marketplace, wishing to hide himself in the midst of the crowd. It happens that at that very moment, bells are ringing and drums are beating as the king’s edicts are proclaimed to capture him.
At that time, the man has no other thought; he thinks only this: 'May I not now be recognized by others and seized and bound. "

The assembly of bodhisattvas is also like this: those who wish to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, if they constantly contemplate the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), will find no opportunity for other mental engagements (*manasikāra*) to arise in between; thus, when these bodhisattvas are practicing, they are not interrupted or intermingled by other states of mind.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
It is like a goldsmith to whom someone brings a hundred pieces of gold and places them in his hands, saying:

'The King has sent this to you, commanding you to fashion various exquisite ornaments. You must apply yourself with diligence and complete them within one month; if they are not finished by the deadline or if they are coarse and inferior, your head shall be cut off, and you will certainly not be pardoned.'"

Upon hearing this, the goldsmith’s body and mind trembled with fear; day and night he applied himself with diligence, exhausting his intellect to fashion the ornaments, never for a moment giving rise to any other thought, but only thinking:
"How shall I complete these regalia as the King has expected?"

Until those ornaments were completed, although that person encountered matters such as food and drink in the interim, they did not form any perception of eating or drinking; rather, their mind remained in continuous succession focused solely upon the gold, contemplating and fashioning it into ornamental objects.
For what reason?
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra,
it is because they cherish their own bodies and lives with extreme affection.
Thereupon, the goldsmith completed the exquisite ornaments according to the appointed time; he brought them to the king's presence and addressed the king, saying:
"The exquisite ornaments for which Your Majesty sent me have now been fully completed."
Upon seeing this, the king was filled with joy and consoled him, saying:
"You have exerted great effort and are able to follow my commands.
While it would normally take twelve months to construct and complete [this], you have been able to accomplish it all within a single month."
Thereupon, he bestowed many gifts upon them as rewards.

It is the same for the assembly of Bodhisattvas: from the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment until the moment the final diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) is about to manifest, they never allow any other thoughts to intervene; they seek only to bring forth the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Just as that goldsmith, out of regard for his own life, never allows any other thought to intervene in the process of crafting the ornaments until they are fully completed;

so too is the Bodhisattva: because he prizes *bodhi*, until he realizes unsurpassed *bodhi*, his mind constantly contemplates the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), and no other mental engagement arises in the interim. This is what is called "the mind being free from intervening thoughts."

“If bodhisattvas seeking all-knowledge can abide in such an uninterrupted and unadulterated mind, practicing with diligence and proceeding toward the conduct of enlightenment, they will swiftly fulfill the provisions for enlightenment.”

While other assemblies of bodhisattvas must pass through incalculable eons, practicing the bodhisattva path with intermittent and distracted minds before they can fulfill the provisions for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, this assembly of bodhisattvas is able to fulfill them without passing even a hundred eons.
Why is this? Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

Because these bodhisattvas seek all-knowledge (sarvajñatā), no other mental engagements can arise for even a moment to intermingle with their great mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta). Therefore, by practicing the bodhisattva path with an unmixed mind, they are able to fulfill the provisions for realizing unsurpassed enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) without passing through a hundred kalpas.
A mind that is interrupted and mixed continues for a long time, yet it cannot accomplish the provisions for enlightenment;
a mind that is uninterrupted and unmixed continues for only a short time, yet it can accomplish the provisions for enlightenment because it constantly progresses from moment to moment.

Thus, a bodhisattva who seeks unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and wishes to swiftly fulfill the accumulations should diligently apply skillful means to correctly induce an uninterrupted and undistracted mind; if one attains such a mind, it will be easy to realize the knowledge of all aspects.
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked Śāriputra:
"What is the nature of an uninterrupted mind?
What kind of mental attention (*manasikāra*) can interrupt the mind, such that by means of it, the mind is said to be 'interrupted'?"
"How do the assembly of bodhisattvas avoid this?
Śāriputra replied, "If bodhisattvas seek all-knowledge through skillful means, they have no other mental engagements to intermingle in the interim; their nature is one of an uninterrupted mind."
If one’s mental attention is associated with the Śrāvaka vehicle,

or if it is associated with the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and these are all interspersed with the mind of great enlightenment (mahābodhicitta), they are all termed the bodhisattva’s improper mental attention (ayoniśomanasikāra).

Why is this? Because the mental orientations of the two vehicles are contrary to and detrimental to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. If such a mind arises and manifests before one, one will be unable to fulfill the provisions for enlightenment, as one will instead delight in nirvāṇa and feel aversion toward saṃsāra.
A bodhisattva should avoid those [states] from afar, reflecting thus:
"The mental orientations of the two vehicles oppose omniscience and accord with parinirvāṇa; my mind should not be interspersed with them."
"Therefore, a bodhisattva should form this thought:

'Although a mind associated with greed, hatred, and delusion constitutes an obstacle to great enlightenment, it can still accord with the provisions for enlightenment; it is not extremely mixed with the mind of a bodhisattva in the same way as the mind that seeks the stages of a pratyekabuddha or a śrāvaka.'"
Why is this? Because greed, hatred, delusion, and the like cause the continuity of all existences within birth and death, yet they assist the bodhisattvas in bringing forth all-knowledge.
That is to say, through their skillful means, the assembly of bodhisattvas gives rise to afflictions and undergoes future bodies of existence, [working] together with all...

They bring great benefit to sentient beings; by relying upon them, they cultivate and bring to perfection the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom;
by relying upon them, they cultivate and bring to perfection the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; by relying upon them...
One trains in and brings to perfection the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power,
the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path; based on these,
one trains in and brings to perfection the gateways to liberation— emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness— and based on these, one trains in the dhāraṇīs.

He brings the doors of liberation and the doors of samādhi to full perfection; relying upon these, he trains in and brings to full perfection the bodhisattva stages, the five eyes, and the six supernormal powers;

and relying upon these, he trains in and brings to full perfection the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity.
Furthermore, they bring to full completion the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha and other immeasurable, boundless buddha-qualities.

In this way, these afflictions assist the bodhisattva in realizing unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; they do not function as the mental orientations of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, for such mental orientations obstruct great enlightenment and hinder the accumulations from reaching fulfillment.
"Therefore, when the assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas gives rise to that distracted mind of mental engagement, unsurpassed bodhi becomes even more remote.

Consequently, the distracted minds of Bodhisattvas are no different from the mental engagements of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; the assembly of Bodhisattvas seeking great bodhi should avoid them from afar and not allow them to arise even for a moment."
The mental attention toward afflictions accords with the various bodies of existence, yet it does not excessively intermingle with the bodhisattva’s mind.
Why is this? O Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

The assembly of bodhisattvas, seeking great enlightenment and donning the armor of diligence in order to deliver sentient beings, dwell for a long time within saṃsāra to bring about great benefit; they should not hastily sever their mental engagement with the afflictions.

When this mental attention manifests before one, it causes all sentient beings to maintain a long-term continuity; based upon this, they are able to fully perfect the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as well as all other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas.

In this way, attention associated with afflictions that leads to future existence assists bodhisattvas in bringing forth unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; until they have realized enlightenment, they should not seek to abandon it, and even until they sit upon the sublime seat of enlightenment, they should never extinguish this attention.
"Therefore, when afflictions arise and manifest before Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, they should not give rise to extreme aversion toward them. Why is this? "
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
The assembly of bodhisattvas conceives the thought that all afflictions are their benefactors, reflecting thus:
"It is because of them that I am able to bring forth and swiftly perfect the various provisions for enlightenment; therefore, they possess great kindness and virtue toward me."
Why is this so? Just as other wholesome dharmas that are beneficial to me should be cherished and respected, so too with the afflictions; one should not loathe them.

"In this way, through their skillful means, bodhisattvas feel deep love and reverence for all afflictions and their objects as well, just as they do for the Buddha, the World-Honored One. Why is this so? "
These bodhisattvas, through their skillful means, reflect as follows:

"Because the fetters of existence have not yet been permanently severed, I am able to practice the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as well as all other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas, bringing them all to fulfillment; by this, I shall bring forth the knowledge of all modes."

Whenever the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as well as other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas, are gradually brought to full completion, at those very times the fetters of existence become increasingly attenuated until they are entirely exhausted, whereby one realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

“It is, for example, like a merchant who loads his cart with various kinds of wealth and treasures and travels far toward a great city. From time to time as the cart rolls forward and gradually advances, from time to time its hubs, rims, and axles gradually wear down and become thin. In this way, by proceeding step by step, he succeeds in entering the great city; yet once the cart has finally broken apart all at once, the owner, having accomplished his purpose, has no further concern for it.”

In this way, through the bodhisattva’s skillful means, they take up the basis of the personal existence by means of the fetters (*saṃyojana*). Whenever the continuum of personal existence is taken up by the fetters, at those very times the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as well as other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas, gradually reach fulfillment.

Whenever the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as well as other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas, gradually reach fulfillment, at those very times all the fetters of existence (*bhava-saṃyojana*) are gradually attenuated.
Whenever all the fetters of existence are gradually attenuated, at those very times one progressively draws near to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

When a Bodhisattva realizes great enlightenment, at that time the fetters (saṃyojana) of the body upon which he relies are all exhausted; having completed what was to be done, he no longer requires the fetters of the body, just as a carriage is no longer needed once one has already entered the city.
Although such afflictions constitute obstacles to great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), they possess the capacity to assist in bringing forth the accumulations for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*).
Therefore, a bodhisattva does not permanently eliminate them until sitting upon the seat of sublime enlightenment; once enlightenment is attained, they are all severed instantaneously.

If there are sentient beings who come to the Bodhisattva and first severely revile and disparage him, only afterwards begging for wealth or the Dharma, the Bodhisattva at that time joyfully bestows it upon them, thinking:
"Now this sentient being has come to me and bestowed great kindness and virtue upon me, enabling me to accomplish generosity and patience, through which I shall realize the knowledge of all modes."
"Because of that, I give rise to a superior resolve (*adhyāśaya*) and proceed toward great enlightenment, which is superior to other objects.
