Thus, among all the mental orientations (*manasikāra*) of a bodhisattva, with the exception of those associated with the two vehicles, he does not reject any other mental orientations, for there is none among them that does not possess the power of assistance in realizing the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).
Then, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:
"Is it not the case that the two vehicles also provide assistance toward omniscience?

For instance, the śrāvakas are also able to instruct and admonish bodhisattvas, causing them to diligently train in the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as well as other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas. Furthermore, the pratyekabuddhas also serve as fields of merit; when the assembly of bodhisattvas gives them clothing and food, they are able to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes."
"How can it be said that the mental attention associated with Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas is incapable of providing assistance toward omniscience and its provisions?
At that time, Śāriputra replied to the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra: "It is so!"

It is so! Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas also provide assistance toward omniscience and its provisions; that is to say, śrāvakas are also able to instruct and admonish bodhisattvas, causing them to diligently practice and train in the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

They are also able to instruct and admonish bodhisattvas, causing them to diligently practice and study internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature;
they are also able to instruct and admonish bodhisattvas, causing them to diligently practice and study the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions.

They are also able to instruct and admonish bodhisattvas, causing them to diligently practice and study the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path;

they are also able to instruct and admonish bodhisattvas, causing them to diligently practice and study the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten universal bases;
they are also able to instruct and admonish bodhisattvas, causing them to diligently practice and study the gates of liberation: emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

They are also able to instruct and admonish bodhisattvas, causing them to diligently cultivate and study the Stage of Extreme Joy, the Stage of Purity, the Stage of Radiant Light, the Stage of Blazing Wisdom, the Stage of Difficult Victory, the Stage of Presence, the Stage of Far-Going, the Immovable Stage, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence, and the Stage of the Dharma Cloud;

they are also able to instruct and admonish bodhisattvas, causing them to diligently cultivate and study the Stage of Pure Observation, the Stage of Seed-Nature, the Eighth Stage, the Stage of Possessing Vision, the Stage of Thinness, the Stage of Freedom from Desire, the Stage of Completion, the Stage of Pratyekabuddhas, the Stage of Bodhisattvas, and the Stage of Tathāgatas;
and they are also able to instruct and admonish bodhisattvas, causing them to diligently cultivate and study the gateways of dhāraṇīs and the gateways of samādhis.
They are also able to instruct and admonish bodhisattvas, causing them to diligently practice and study the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;

they are also able to instruct and admonish bodhisattvas, causing them to diligently practice and study the Tathāgata’s ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
they are also able to instruct and admonish bodhisattvas, causing them to diligently practice and study the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs.
They are also able to instruct and admonish bodhisattvas, causing them to diligently practice and study the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity;

they are also able to instruct and admonish bodhisattvas, causing them to diligently practice and study all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);
they are also able to instruct and admonish bodhisattvas, causing them to diligently practice and study all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
They are also able to instruct and admonish bodhisattvas, causing them to diligently train in the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of all buddhas.
Therefore, śrāvakas also provide assistance regarding omniscience and its provisions.

"If Pratyekabuddhas can serve as fields of merit to receive the offerings of Bodhisattvas—meaning that Bodhisattvas, taking those Pratyekabuddhas as their field of merit, dedicate the material requisites of their offerings toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment—therefore, Pratyekabuddhas also provide assistance regarding omniscience and its provisions."
"However, the mental engagements (*manasikāra*) of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas provide no assistance whatsoever toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) or its provisions (*sambhāra*). Why is this?

The mental engagements associated with Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas provide superior assistance regarding the stages of the two vehicles, yet they are utterly incompatible with the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment sought by Bodhisattvas and their provisions; that is to say, they involve weariness with saṃsāra and a longing for parinirvāṇa, thereby abandoning great enlightenment and sentient beings."

Therefore, it is prescribed that a bodhisattva in meditative concentration should not give rise to mental orientations associated with pratyekabuddhas or śrāvakas, for such mental orientations are incompatible with both the buddhahood sought by bodhisattvas and the sentient beings they aim to benefit.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

All those belonging to the Śrāvaka vehicle possess great merit toward the assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who seek unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. This is because they proclaim to the assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas the teachings corresponding to all the pāramitās and other sublime practices, providing instructions and admonitions so that they may diligently train and swiftly attain perfection. Furthermore, they act as pure fields of merit for the Bodhisattvas, receiving their offerings and causing the Bodhisattvas to quickly bring the provisions for enlightenment to fulfillment."

Because of this, the śrāvakas possess great merit toward all bodhisattvas; therefore, through their skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), bodhisattvas observe that for all sentient beings and all phenomena, there is nothing that does not possess the merit of being conducive to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and its provisions (*sambhāra*).

“The wisdom and mind of the arhats are also beneficial to those of the bodhisattva vehicle; for if they did not exist, there would be nothing to be avoided. How, then, can it be said that bodhisattvas should not give rise to the mind of an arhat, nor should they cultivate the wisdom of an arhat?”
By way of negating that [view], the bodhisattva brings the accumulations for enlightenment to swift fulfillment and is able to rapidly realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).

Therefore, the wisdom and mind of the arhat also possess merit for the Bodhisattvayāna; that is to say, they enable the bodhisattva to attain omniscience and to bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings until the end of the future.

The wisdom and mind of all pratyekabuddhas also possess merit for those of the bodhisattva vehicle; for if they did not exist, there would be nothing to be excluded. How then could it be said that bodhisattvas should not give rise to the mind of the pratyekabuddha vehicle, nor should they cultivate the wisdom of the pratyekabuddha vehicle?
By means of negating those [extremes], the bodhisattva brings the accumulations for awakening to swift fulfillment and is able to rapidly realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).

Therefore, whether it be the wisdom or the mind of the pratyekabuddhas, they also possess merit and virtue toward the bodhisattva vehicle; that is to say, they enable the bodhisattva to attain omniscience and to bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings until the end of the future.
Furthermore, one observes that the mental faculties of those of the two vehicles are inferior, whereas Bodhisattvas cultivate and study superior mental faculties;
if the mental faculties of the two vehicles were not inferior, Bodhisattvas would have no need to cultivate the superior.

Whether it be the mind or the wisdom of all bodhisattvas—whether with outflows or without outflows—with the exception of the mind or wisdom of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, among all others, it is the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the highest, the most sublime, the most exquisite, the superior, the unsurpassed, the unequaled, and the equal to the unequaled.
Therefore, whether it be the wisdom or the mind of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, there exists at least a slight degree of conforming power toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

Likewise, through their skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), bodhisattvas contemplate all sentient beings and all phenomena, seeing that they possess a conforming power toward both omniscience and its provisions; thus, they never grow weary of or abandon any state of mind.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of generosity, although they engage in the relinquishing of precious wealth and other such things, they do not harbor perceptions that grasp at those objects. That is to say, if they relinquish all signs of phenomena (*dharma-nimitta*) and dedicate [the merit] toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, desiring to bring great benefit to sentient beings, they will be able to realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).
However, if they do not relinquish signs when dedicating toward enlightenment, yet desire to bring great benefit to sentient beings, they will ultimately never attain the knowledge of all modes."
"If bodhisattvas are able to obtain various treasures such as gold and silver, although this is called gaining profit, it is not yet called attaining great benefit.
If bodhisattvas are able to relinquish various treasures such as gold and silver, only then can it be called attaining great benefit."

If bodhisattvas are able to relinquish all signs and dedicate [their merit] toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, desiring to bring great benefit to sentient beings, they are said to be able to attain unsurpassed, sublime benefit.

"If bodhisattvas become universal monarchs (cakravartin kings), ruling over the four continents and attaining great sovereignty, although they obtain fame and profit, this is not yet called attaining the great benefit."
If bodhisattvas relinquish the sovereignty of a universal monarch over the four continents, this may be called attaining a great benefit.

However, if bodhisattvas can relinquish all marks and dedicate [their merit] toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, desiring to bring great benefit to sentient beings, this is called attaining the unsurpassed, sublime benefit.

"If a bodhisattva becomes a king of the desire realm, exercising sovereign control over the desire realm and attaining great mastery, although he may be said to have gained renown and profit, he is not yet said to have attained great benefit."
If bodhisattvas are able to renounce the sovereign kingship of the desire realm, they may be said to have attained great benefit.

If bodhisattvas are able to renounce all marks and dedicate [their merit] toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, desiring to bring about great benefit for sentient beings, they are said to have attained unsurpassed, virtuous benefit.

"If sentient beings abandon all marks and attain the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of arhatship, or the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, although they are said to have gained benefit, they are not yet said to have been able to gain the great benefit."

If sentient beings relinquish all signs and dedicate [their merit] toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, desiring to bring great benefit to sentient beings, they are said to be able to attain unsurpassed, sublime benefit.
"If one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, it will be the most supreme and most excellent among all benefits, with nothing able to equal it. Why is this so?"

The unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment sought by the assembly of bodhisattvas is able to bring great benefit to sentient beings; for śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and ordinary worldlings, this capacity does not exist.

"If a bodhisattva universally takes as their object of focus all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their assemblies of disciples throughout the ten directions, and offers various kinds of excellent food and drink, clothing, bedding, medicinal requisites for illness, dwellings, wealth, flowers, incense, and other such items as gifts and offerings—although this is called obtaining benefit, it is not yet called obtaining the unsurpassed benefit."

If bodhisattvas are able to relinquish all signs and dedicate [their merit] toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, desiring to bring great benefit to sentient beings, they are said to be able to attain unsurpassed, sublime benefit.

Why is this so? Because objects such as food and drink all possess manifold characteristics (*nimitta*); all phenomena possessing characteristics have quantity and number; and because phenomena with quantity and number have limitations, one cannot, by relying upon them, realize the limitless wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*).

"If Bodhisattvas, through skillful means, take as their object all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their assemblies of disciples throughout the worlds of the ten directions—possessing immeasurable kinds of rare and marvelous qualities—yet do not grasp at signs;

and although they conceive of boundless, supreme food and drink, clothing, bedding, medicinal requisites for illness, dwellings, wealth, flowers, incense, and other such items to offer as gifts and worship, yet do not grasp at signs;
and although they are able to dedicate [the merit] toward unsurpassed enlightenment, desiring to bring great benefit to sentient beings, yet do not grasp at signs;"

By means of this, one realizes the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) and benefits sentient beings until the end of the future; this should be known as attaining the unsurpassed benefit, which is the foremost among all benefits.

If bodhisattvas are able to employ such skillful means while practicing generosity, they are called "bodhisattvas dwelling at the summit," and they will certainly attain the knowledge of all modes of being (*sarvajñajñāna*).

Why is this? Because the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*) is extremely difficult to attain; yet such a bodhisattva is able to relinquish all internal and external marks, with a mind free from attachment, seeking to realize such knowledge of all-knowledge. Among all bodhisattvas, they are the most preeminent, and shall attain unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), which is like the crown of the head.

All bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present who have attained, will attain, or are currently attaining the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) do so without exception by means of the skillful means (upāyakauśalya) thus generated.
Then, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked the venerable Śāriputra:
"In what way does a bodhisattva come to enter the ranks of those bodhisattvas who dwell at the summit? Śāriputra replied:
“If bodhisattvas, through skillful means, do not grasp at the marks of phenomena, these bodhisattvas attain entry into the rank of those bodhisattvas who dwell at the summit.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked:
“In what phenomena do these bodhisattvas not grasp at what marks?”

Śāriputra said: "These bodhisattvas do not apprehend the characteristics of permanence or impermanence in the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), nor do they apprehend the characteristics of permanence or impermanence in the aggregates of feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

They do not apprehend the characteristics of pleasure or suffering in the aggregate of form, nor do they apprehend the characteristics of pleasure or suffering in the aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness."

Regarding the aggregate of form, one does not grasp at the marks of self or non-self; regarding the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, one likewise does not grasp at the marks of self or non-self.

Regarding the aggregate of form, one does not grasp at the marks of purity or impurity; regarding the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, one likewise does not grasp at the marks of purity or impurity.

Regarding the aggregate of form, one does not grasp at the marks of detachment or non-detachment; regarding the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, one likewise does not grasp at the marks of detachment or non-detachment.

One does not grasp at the signs of tranquility or non-tranquility regarding the aggregate of form; nor does one grasp at the signs of tranquility or non-tranquility regarding the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

"These bodhisattvas do not apprehend the marks of permanence or impermanence in the sense-base of the eye, nor do they apprehend the marks of permanence or impermanence in the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind;

they do not apprehend the marks of pleasure or suffering in the sense-base of the eye, nor do they apprehend the marks of pleasure or suffering in the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind;
they do not apprehend the marks of self or non-self in the sense-base of the eye, nor do they apprehend the marks of self or non-self in the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind."
One does not grasp at signs of purity or impurity regarding the sense base of the eye;
nor does one grasp at signs of purity or impurity regarding the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.

One does not grasp at signs of detachment or non-detachment regarding the sense base of the eye; nor does one grasp at signs of detachment or non-detachment regarding the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.

One does not apprehend the characteristic of tranquility or non-tranquility in the sense-base of the eye; nor does one apprehend the characteristic of tranquility or non-tranquility in the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.

"These bodhisattvas do not apprehend the marks of permanence or impermanence regarding the sphere of form; they likewise do not apprehend the marks of permanence or impermanence regarding the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena.

They do not apprehend the marks of pleasure or suffering regarding the sphere of form; they likewise do not apprehend the marks of pleasure or suffering regarding the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena.

They do not apprehend the marks of self or non-self regarding the sphere of form; they likewise do not apprehend the marks of self or non-self regarding the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena."

One does not grasp at signs of purity or impurity regarding the sense base of form; nor does one grasp at signs of purity or impurity regarding the sense bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena.

One does not grasp at signs of remoteness or non-remoteness regarding the sense base of form; nor does one grasp at signs of remoteness or non-remoteness regarding the sense bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena.

One does not grasp at signs of tranquility or non-tranquility regarding the sense base of form; nor does one grasp at signs of tranquility or non-tranquility regarding the sense bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena.

"These bodhisattvas do not apprehend the marks of permanence or impermanence in the eye-element; nor do they apprehend the marks of permanence or impermanence in the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-element.
They do not apprehend the marks of pleasure or suffering in the eye-element; nor do they apprehend the marks of pleasure or suffering in the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-element.
They do not apprehend the marks of self or non-self in the eye-element; nor do they apprehend the marks of self or non-self in the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-element."
One does not grasp at signs of purity or impurity regarding the eye-element; nor does one grasp at signs of purity or impurity regarding the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-element.

One does not grasp at signs of detachment or non-detachment regarding the eye-element; nor does one grasp at signs of detachment or non-detachment regarding the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-element.

One does not grasp at signs of tranquility or non-tranquility regarding the eye-element; nor does one grasp at signs of tranquility or non-tranquility regarding the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-element.

"These bodhisattvas do not grasp at the marks of permanence or impermanence regarding the realm of form; they likewise do not grasp at the marks of permanence or impermanence regarding the realms of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena.

They do not grasp at the marks of pleasure or suffering regarding the realm of form; they likewise do not grasp at the marks of pleasure or suffering regarding the realms of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena.

They do not grasp at the marks of self or non-self regarding the realm of form; they likewise do not grasp at the marks of self or non-self regarding the realms of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena."

In the realm of form, one does not grasp at signs of purity or impurity; likewise, in the realms of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena, one also does not grasp at signs of purity or impurity.

In the realm of form, one does not grasp at signs of detachment or non-detachment; likewise, in the realms of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena, one also does not grasp at signs of detachment or non-detachment.

In the realm of form, one does not grasp at signs of tranquility or non-tranquility; likewise, in the realms of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena, one also does not grasp at signs of tranquility or non-tranquility.

"These bodhisattvas do not grasp at the marks of permanence or impermanence regarding the eye-consciousness element; they likewise do not grasp at the marks of permanence or impermanence regarding the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements.

They do not grasp at the marks of pleasure or suffering regarding the eye-consciousness element; they likewise do not grasp at the marks of pleasure or suffering regarding the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements.

They do not grasp at the marks of self or non-self regarding the eye-consciousness element; they likewise do not grasp at the marks of self or non-self regarding the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements."

One does not grasp at signs of purity or impurity regarding the eye-consciousness element; nor does one grasp at signs of purity or impurity regarding the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-consciousness elements.

One does not grasp at signs of detachment or non-detachment regarding the eye-consciousness element; nor does one grasp at signs of detachment or non-detachment regarding the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-consciousness elements.

One does not grasp at signs of tranquility or non-tranquility regarding the eye-consciousness element; nor does one grasp at signs of tranquility or non-tranquility regarding the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-consciousness elements.

"These bodhisattvas do not grasp at the marks of permanence or impermanence regarding eye-contact; nor do they grasp at the marks of permanence or impermanence regarding ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact.
They do not grasp at the marks of pleasure or suffering regarding eye-contact; nor do they grasp at the marks of pleasure or suffering regarding ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact.
They do not grasp at the marks of self or non-self regarding eye-contact; nor do they grasp at the marks of self or non-self regarding ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact."
Regarding eye-contact, one does not grasp at signs of purity or impurity; regarding ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact, one likewise does not grasp at signs of purity or impurity.

Regarding eye-contact, one does not grasp at signs of detachment or non-detachment; regarding ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact, one likewise does not grasp at signs of detachment or non-detachment.

Regarding eye-contact, one does not grasp at signs of tranquility or non-tranquility; regarding ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact, one likewise does not grasp at signs of tranquility or non-tranquility.

"These bodhisattvas do not grasp at the signs of permanence or impermanence regarding the feelings produced with eye-contact as condition; nor do they grasp at the signs of permanence or impermanence regarding the feelings produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-contact as condition.

They do not grasp at the signs of pleasure or pain regarding the feelings produced with eye-contact as condition; nor do they grasp at the signs of pleasure or pain regarding the feelings produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-contact as condition.

They do not grasp at the signs of self or non-self regarding the feelings produced with eye-contact as condition; nor do they grasp at the signs of self or non-self regarding the feelings produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-contact as condition."

Regarding the various feelings arising conditioned by eye-contact, one does not grasp at signs of purity or impurity; regarding the various feelings arising conditioned by ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact, one likewise does not grasp at signs of purity or impurity.

Regarding the various feelings arising conditioned by eye-contact, one does not grasp at signs of detachment or non-detachment; regarding the various feelings arising conditioned by ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact, one likewise does not grasp at signs of detachment or non-detachment.

Regarding the various feelings arising conditioned by eye-contact, one does not grasp at signs of tranquility or non-tranquility; regarding the various feelings arising conditioned by ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact, one likewise does not grasp at signs of tranquility or non-tranquility.

"These bodhisattvas do not grasp at the marks of permanence or impermanence regarding the earth element; they likewise do not grasp at the marks of permanence or impermanence regarding the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements.

They do not grasp at the marks of pleasure or suffering regarding the earth element; they likewise do not grasp at the marks of pleasure or suffering regarding the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements.

They do not grasp at the marks of self or non-self regarding the earth element; they likewise do not grasp at the marks of self or non-self regarding the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements."

One does not grasp at the signs of purity or impurity regarding the earth element; nor does one grasp at the signs of purity or impurity regarding the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements.

One does not grasp at the signs of remoteness or non-remoteness regarding the earth element; nor does one grasp at the signs of remoteness or non-remoteness regarding the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements.

One does not grasp at the signs of tranquility or non-tranquility regarding the earth element; nor does one grasp at the signs of tranquility or non-tranquility regarding the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements.

"These bodhisattvas do not grasp at the characteristics of permanence or impermanence regarding the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*); they likewise do not grasp at the characteristics of permanence or impermanence regarding the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

They do not grasp at the characteristics of pleasure or suffering regarding the causal condition; they likewise do not grasp at the characteristics of pleasure or suffering regarding the equal-and-immediate condition, the object-condition, and the dominant condition.

They do not grasp at the characteristics of self or non-self regarding the causal condition; they likewise do not grasp at the characteristics of self or non-self regarding the equal-and-immediate condition, the object-condition, and the dominant condition."

Regarding the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), one does not grasp at signs of purity or impurity; regarding the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), one likewise does not grasp at signs of purity or impurity.

Regarding the causal condition, one does not grasp at signs of separation or non-separation; regarding the equal-and-immediate, objective, and dominant conditions, one likewise does not grasp at signs of separation or non-separation.

Regarding the causal condition, one does not grasp at signs of tranquility or non-tranquility; regarding the equal-and-immediate, objective, and dominant conditions, one likewise does not grasp at signs of tranquility or non-tranquility.

"These bodhisattvas do not grasp at the marks of permanence or impermanence regarding ignorance; nor do they grasp at the marks of permanence or impermanence regarding volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming, birth, or old age and death.

They do not grasp at the marks of pleasure or suffering regarding ignorance; nor do they grasp at the marks of pleasure or suffering regarding volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming, birth, or old age and death.

They do not grasp at the marks of self or non-self regarding ignorance; nor do they grasp at the marks of self or non-self regarding volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming, birth, or old age and death."

One does not grasp at the marks of purity or impurity regarding ignorance; nor does one grasp at the marks of purity or impurity regarding volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, or old age and death.

One does not grasp at the marks of detachment or non-detachment regarding ignorance; nor does one grasp at the marks of detachment or non-detachment regarding volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, or old age and death.

One does not grasp at the marks of tranquility or non-tranquility regarding ignorance; nor does one grasp at the marks of tranquility or non-tranquility regarding volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, or old age and death.

"These bodhisattvas do not grasp at the marks of permanence or impermanence regarding the desire realm; they likewise do not grasp at the marks of permanence or impermanence regarding the form and formless realms.
They do not grasp at the marks of pleasure or suffering regarding the desire realm; they likewise do not grasp at the marks of pleasure or suffering regarding the form and formless realms.
They do not grasp at the marks of self or non-self regarding the desire realm; they likewise do not grasp at the marks of self or non-self regarding the form and formless realms."
In the desire realm, one does not grasp at signs of purity or impurity; in the form and formless realms, one likewise does not grasp at signs of purity or impurity.
In the desire realm, one does not grasp at signs of detachment or non-detachment; in the form and formless realms, one likewise does not grasp at signs of detachment or non-detachment.
In the desire realm, one does not grasp at signs of tranquility or non-tranquility; in the form and formless realms, one likewise does not grasp at signs of tranquility or non-tranquility.

"If bodhisattvas can employ such skillful means as these, practicing the perfection of generosity without grasping at the marks of phenomena, these bodhisattvas shall enter the rank of those bodhisattvas who dwell at the summit, and they shall be able to attain the omniscient wisdom that is like a summit."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If bodhisattvas know that all phenomena are not substantially existent and are free from all signs, yet practice the perfection of generosity, these bodhisattvas attain entry into the rank of bodhisattvas who dwell at the summit; they are able to attain the omniscient wisdom (sarvajñajñāna) which is like a summit, and they are also able to teach and transform all sentient beings, causing them to rely upon such omniscient wisdom to make vows and seek it, and likewise to realize it."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If sentient beings do not give rise to resolute conviction in the signless dharma, they cannot produce the mind of omniscience; if they cannot produce the mind of omniscience, they cannot cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva; and if they cannot cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva, they cannot attain the wisdom of omniscience."

If sentient beings are able to give rise to resolute conviction in signless phenomena, they will be able to generate the mind of omniscience; if they can generate the mind of omniscience, they will be able to practice the various bodhisattva deeds; if they can practice the various bodhisattva deeds, they will be able to realize the wisdom of omniscience.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If bodhisattvas, having resolved their minds to seek all-knowledge, are able to understand that whatever things they relinquish are empty and non-existent as they practice the perfection of giving—meaning they know, according to reality, that all things relinquished are like illusions and transformations, unlike the various marks grasped by us since beginningless time."
Because of this capacity for knowledge, one is able to relinquish all that exists and not grasp at any signs.

Because sentient beings do not know reality as it is—that all phenomena are non-existent and like illusions—they give rise to firm attachment toward all things. Due to this firm attachment, they are unable to relinquish them; due to their failure to relinquish them, they embrace stinginess; and because of this stinginess, when the body perishes and life ends, they fall into the evil destinies and undergo the suffering of poverty.

Whatever one obtains, one is unable to relinquish; furthermore, within that state, one increases stinginess and avarice. Due to this, one again falls into the various evil destinies to undergo manifold sufferings. Such experiences of suffering all arise from grasping at signs.

"If Bodhisattvas possess skillful means, they know that phenomena do not exist and are all like illusions and transformations; since they are like illusions and transformations, they should all be relinquished, for illusions and transformations are neither 'I' nor 'mine. Thus, they are able to relinquish all things."
Why is this? Since the phenomena of "self" and "what belongs to self" cannot be found, one should not cling to them; because there is no clinging, one is able to relinquish them all.
Through this ability to relinquish, one develops a profound love and joy for the sublime Dharma taught by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, thinking as follows:
“Rare indeed, World-Honored One!

You have excellently taught that all phenomena are like illusions and transformations. Relying upon the Buddha’s teaching, I am able to relinquish everything; that is to say, I can cast off phenomena that are like illusions and transformations, so that I may attain the illusory, signless, unsurpassed bodhi.”
These bodhisattvas formed this thought:

"The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are able to perform what is difficult to perform; that is to say, they teach bodhisattvas to understand all phenomena as they truly are—neither existent nor real, but like illusions and transformations. Because of this understanding, they do not give rise to attachment; with little exertion of effort, they are able to relinquish everything and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Therefore, a bodhisattva who wishes to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should understand that all phenomena do not exist and are entirely like illusions and transformations; they should abandon all marks and, with a mind free of marks, diligently seek the omniscient wisdom that is like the crown of the head.
"Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, do not think that these teachings I have spoken are due to my own eloquence; they are entirely through the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Whatever Śāriputra has now spoken is all through the Buddha’s spiritual power. You should receive and uphold it, and after my parinirvāṇa, you should cause it to be widely disseminated."

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 583. Translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree. Part Three of the Eleventh Section on the Perfection of Giving (*Dānapāramitā*). At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"If all phenomena are not truly existent, what is it that Bodhisattvas relinquish when they practice generosity?
The Buddha said,
"When Bodhisattvas practice generosity, there is nothing at all that is relinquished."
Then, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If, when practicing generosity, bodhisattvas relinquish nothing at all, what do these bodhisattvas obtain when they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening?"
The Buddha said:

"When a bodhisattva practices giving, they relinquish nothing at all among all phenomena; likewise, when they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they likewise obtain nothing at all among all phenomena."

Just as when a bodhisattva practices generosity, there is no diminution whatsoever of any phenomenon, so too when a bodhisattva realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, there is no augmentation whatsoever of any phenomenon; for the two gates of diminution and augmentation are established in mutual dependence.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

Just as when bodhisattvas practice generosity, they know that all phenomena are like illusions and transformations, having no reality that can be relinquished; so too, when such bodhisattvas realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they know that all phenomena are likewise like illusions and transformations, having no reality that can be attained."

If, when bodhisattvas practice generosity, they were to actually relinquish anything among all phenomena, then when those bodhisattvas realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they would likewise actually obtain something among phenomena.

However, when Bodhisattvas practice giving, there is in reality nothing among all phenomena that is relinquished; therefore, when Bodhisattvas realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, there is in reality nothing among all phenomena that is attained.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
It is like two illusionists performing a trade by magic: one creates a high price, while the other conjures a beautiful ball of rice; herein, both matters are equally non-existent as reality."

In this way, when a bodhisattva practices giving, they relinquish things that are like illusions and transformations, lacking true existence; and when they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they attain dharmas that are like illusions and transformations, lacking true existence.
When these bodhisattvas practice giving, there is in reality no loss; when they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, there is likewise no real gain.

Although these bodhisattvas appear to suffer loss while practicing giving, in truth there is no loss; although they appear to gain benefit when realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, in truth there is no gain.

Just as that illusionist relinquishes the price of the illusion—though it appears to be a loss, there is in fact no loss—so too when a bodhisattva practices generosity, he relinquishes what is not a real thing; though it appears to be a loss, there is in fact no loss.

Just as when a magician produces an illusory lump of meat, which appears to be beneficial but is actually of no benefit, so too when a bodhisattva realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, it appears to be beneficial but is actually of no benefit.
In this way, the dharma and its analogy correspond in cause and effect; those who possess wisdom should understand this correctly.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
It is like a skilled illusionist or his disciple who, at a crossroads, conjures a woman. Suddenly she appears pregnant and soon gives birth to a son, but that son dies shortly thereafter."
"What do you think?
When that woman’s son was born, did she experience joy, and when he died, did she experience sorrow?
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra replied:
“Both she and her child exist as illusions; in reality, there is neither birth nor death. Who, then, could feel sorrow or joy on account of whom?
The Buddha said, “It is so!”
It is as you have said.

It is likewise for the assembly of bodhisattvas: when practicing generosity, there is neither relinquishing nor loss; when realizing unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, there is neither attainment nor benefit.

Therefore, when a bodhisattva practices generosity, although there is something relinquished, no sorrow arises; and when they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, although there is something attained, no joy arises, because they know that what is relinquished and what is attained are like illusions and transformations.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra! What do you think?
Do you consider that the Tathāgata has great desire for all wholesome dharmas?"
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:
“No, World-Honored One!”
"No, Sugata! Why is that?"
"All dharmas realized by the Tathāgata are empty; the Tathāgata who can realize those dharmas is also empty, because within emptiness there is neither desire nor that which is desired.
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
It is as you have said.
Because the Tathāgata perceives that all phenomena are empty, there is no great desire even within wholesome dharmas; just as I now have no mind of desire whatsoever toward any phenomenon.
Although the Bodhisattva practiced giving in the past, he relinquished nothing at all regarding all phenomena, for he thoroughly understood that all phenomena are ultimately empty.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, harbor neither attachment nor aversion toward any phenomenon.
"Why is this? Because they have realized that all phenomena are not substantially existent, being by nature empty and quiescent, and because craving and aversion have been severed.
At that time, Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How marvelous!
World-Honored One! How rare!"

"Sugata! To the extent that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to relinquish phenomena, to that same extent they realize them all as empty, false and unreal, lacking inherent solidity, devoid of autonomous function, and free from any attachment."

"As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, although Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas may give to sentient beings the world-systems filled with precious jewels as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they do not form this thought within themselves:
'I am able to relinquish and give away so many precious jewels.'"
"Although he has no attachment therein, he causes the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) to be swiftly fulfilled.

In this way, the bodhisattva can take the roots of virtue accumulated through generosity and dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Having performed this act, he gives rise to this thought:
'It is the nature of a bodhisattva to relinquish everything; although I now relinquish the things that ought to be relinquished, the things relinquished are all like illusions and transformations.'"

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can understand in this way, that bodhisattva mahāsattva enters the ranks of the bodhisattvas; though they relinquish all things, there is nothing relinquished, and though they attain all things, there is nothing attained.

If bodhisattvas cannot understand this as it truly is, they are not genuine bodhisattvas; they will be unable to relinquish material wealth or the Dharma, and they will be unable to realize great enlightenment.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:
"With what kind of mind should bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice giving?
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra replied:
“Venerable Śāriputra!
You have first explained this meaning for us; we, too, shall speak briefly on this matter.”
Then, Śāriputra addressed the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, saying:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, that bodhisattva mahāsattva should first contemplate the ultimate emptiness and quiescence of the nature of all phenomena; next, they should contemplate the supreme merits possessed by the knowledge of all modes; and finally, they should take pity on all sentient beings who lack precious wealth and undergo various sufferings. Having formed this thought, they should then relinquish everything."

Whether they be possessions that are grasped or ungrasped, internal or external, all such precious wealth he gives to sentient beings with a mind free from attachment; he also bestows the true Dharma upon sentient beings, and furthermore, he reverently makes offerings to the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha with boundless, supreme, and exquisite requisites.
In this way, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice giving, they should give with a mind focused on omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and free from attachment.
Such giving accords with enlightenment; it enables them to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) and brings great benefit to all sentient beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should contemplate the emptiness of phenomena; they should possess supreme merit by taking all-knowledge as their object, and they should practice generosity with compassion for sentient beings, their minds free from attachment.
If one can practice giving in this manner, one will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, bringing great benefit to all sentient beings.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
"Do you now wish to see the bodhisattvas' acts of giving throughout the worlds of the ten directions?
Śāriputra replied, "Indeed, I wish to see them!"

At that time, Śāriputra and the great assembly, sustained by the Buddha’s spiritual power, beheld to the east, beyond a hundred worlds, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Mahāskandha, surrounded by a great assembly of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, proclaiming the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā) and its supreme merits and great fruits.

In that place there was a bodhisattva named Unobstructed (Anāvaraṇa). Although he lived as a householder, he was free from all attachments; he renounced all his possessions and gave them as alms to all. He accumulated heaps of precious jewels as vast as mountains and bestowed them upon sentient beings according to their needs. Having encouraged other beings to enjoy these things themselves, he would further give them away to others. His mind was unimpeded, and thus he practiced giving without any defilement or attachment, exerting himself day and night without ever becoming weary.

Thus he accumulated clothing, bedding, food, drink, and other such items, each in quantities as vast as mountains; he bestowed them all according to the needs of sentient beings, encouraging others to enjoy them themselves and then further giving them on to others. His mind was free from obstruction; practicing such generosity without attachment, he remained diligent day and night, never wearying.

At that time, Śāriputra and the great assembly all again beheld the Bodhisattva Unobstructed with seven-jeweled carriages, each adorned with hundreds of thousands of gold pieces. Each carriage carried one "jewel-woman," who was of upright appearance and variously adorned; each jewel-woman was attended by a hundred female servants, each riding in a carriage decorated with many jewels. Upon each carriage were placed hundreds of thousands of gold pieces and all necessary provisions, nothing lacking.
They stood at the marketplace and cried out in a loud voice: "Whoever needs these, take them as you please!"
"Practicing giving in this manner, he is free from any attachment, remaining diligent day and night without ever becoming weary.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"Do you see the Bodhisattva Unobstructed in the eastern direction practicing giving with a mind free from attachment?"
Then, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I have seen them,
World-Honored One!”
“I have seen them, Sugata!
the Buddha said.
“Bodhisattvas seeking great enlightenment should all practice giving in this manner.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, what do you think?”
"Does the Bodhisattva Unobstructed practice vast giving? Śāriputra replied, "Vast!"
World-Honored One! Vast! Sugata!
“The measure of the roots of goodness from the Bodhisattva Unobstructed’s giving is boundless.
The Buddha said, “So it is!”
It is as you have said.

If there is a bodhisattva who can contemplate the emptiness of phenomena and, taking all-knowledge as their object, possesses supreme merit, then out of compassion for sentient beings, whatever gift they bestow shall be a hundred times superior, a thousand times superior, and even up to *upaniṣad*-fold superior to the merit obtained from the gift given to the Bodhisattva Unobstructed in the eastern direction.

At that time, Śāriputra and the great assembly, sustained by the Buddha’s spiritual power, again beheld hundreds of thousands of worlds in the eastern direction. In each and every world, there were immeasurable bodhisattvas who each relinquished all they possessed to practice universal giving. They accumulated heaps of precious treasures as vast as mountains and bestowed them upon sentient beings according to their needs. Having encouraged sentient beings to enjoy these things themselves, they further gave them away to others; their minds were free from obstruction. Thus practicing generosity without attachment, they applied themselves with diligence day and night, never wearying.

In this way, he accumulated clothing, bedding, food, drink, and other requisites in quantities as vast as mountains; he bestowed them all according to the needs of sentient beings, and having exhorted others to enjoy them themselves, he further gave them away to others. His mind was free from obstruction; thus practicing such generosity without attachment, he remained diligent day and night, never wearying.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"Do you see, in each of the hundreds of thousands of worlds in the eastern direction, the immeasurable bodhisattvas who practice giving with minds free from attachment?"
Then, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I have seen them,
World-Honored One!”
“I have seen them, Sugata!
