They saw countless bodhisattvas seated upon the seat of enlightenment, and so forth, until they saw countless bodhisattvas subduing immeasurable celestial Māras and enemies, causing them to retreat and disperse, and subsequently realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

By the spiritual power of the Buddha, he further beheld worlds in the northeast as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Ganges Rivers, where countless Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas were proclaiming to the assembly of Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas that the characteristics of permanence and impermanence regarding the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) cannot be apprehended; they proclaimed that the characteristics of permanence and impermanence regarding the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-, saṃjñā-, saṃskāra-, vijñānaskandha*) likewise cannot be apprehended. This was explained at length, until it was said that countless Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, by means of their supernormal powers, travel to other immeasurable and boundless worlds, employing skillful means to benefit, bring peace, and provide happiness to immeasurable sentient beings.
At that time, Śāriputra, seeing such a marvel, was filled with joy and leaped for gladness, and he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How extraordinary!
World-Honored One!”
"How marvelous!
Well-gone One!

You have accomplished such great majestic spiritual power that you enable us to see, in the northeastern direction, worlds as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Gaṅgā rivers, where countless bodhisattva-mahāsattvas perform the various distinct practices of the bodhisattva path, and where countless Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas benefit sentient beings through various skillful means."
How extraordinary!
World-Honored One! How rare!

"Sugata! The Buddhas have accomplished the vast and sublime Dharma, which enables Bodhisattvas to resolve their minds and seek the vast and sublime Dharma accomplished by all Buddhas—namely, unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.

The Buddhas have accomplished the vast and sublime Dharma, which enables Bodhisattvas to resolve their minds and seek the vast and sublime Dharma accomplished by the Buddhas—namely, unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
through this, they are able to cultivate the perfection of the provisions and swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

At that time, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, Śāriputra and the great assembly again beheld, in the direction below, worlds as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Gaṅgā rivers, where countless bodhisattvas sat upon the seat of enlightenment. They saw, in full detail, up to the point where countless bodhisattvas had subdued immeasurable Māras, celestial and demonic adversaries, causing them to retreat and disperse, and subsequently realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

By the spiritual power of the Buddha, they further beheld worlds in the direction below as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Ganges Rivers, where countless Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas were teaching assemblies of Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas that the characteristics of permanence and impermanence regarding the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) cannot be apprehended, and that the characteristics of permanence and impermanence regarding the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-, saṃjñā-, saṃskāra-, vijñāna-skandha*) likewise cannot be apprehended; and so on extensively until: countless Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, through their supernormal powers, traveled to other immeasurable and boundless worlds, employing skillful means to bring benefit, peace, and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings.
At that time, Śāriputra, seeing such a thing, was filled with joy and leaped for gladness, and he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How marvelous!
World-Honored One!”
"How marvelous! O Sugata!

You have accomplished such great majestic spiritual power that you enable us to behold the worlds below, as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Ganges Rivers, and the various distinctions in the bodhisattva practices performed by countless bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as well as the various skillful means through which countless Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas benefit sentient beings."
"How marvelous!
World-Honored One! How rare!"

"Sugata! The Buddhas have accomplished the vast and sublime Dharma, enabling Bodhisattvas to resolve their minds and seek the vast and sublime Dharma accomplished by the Buddhas—namely, unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said.

The Buddhas have accomplished the vast and sublime Dharma, which enables Bodhisattvas to resolve their minds upon seeking the vast and sublime Dharma accomplished by the Buddhas—namely, unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
through this, they are able to cultivate the perfection of the provisions and swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes.

At that time, by the Buddha’s supernatural power, Śāriputra and the great assembly again beheld worlds in the direction of the zenith, as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Gaṅgā Rivers. They saw countless bodhisattvas seated upon the seat of enlightenment, and so forth, until they saw countless bodhisattvas subduing immeasurable celestial Māras and adversaries, causing them to retreat and disperse, and subsequently realizing unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

By the power of the Buddha’s spiritual authority, he further beheld worlds in the direction of the zenith as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Ganges Rivers. There, countless Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas were teaching assemblies of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas that the characteristics of permanence and impermanence regarding the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) cannot be apprehended; they taught that the characteristics of permanence and impermanence regarding the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-, saṃjñā-, saṃskāra-, vijñāna-skandha*) likewise cannot be apprehended. Extending thus, he saw countless Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas using their supernormal powers to travel to other immeasurable and boundless worlds, employing skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) to bring benefit, peace, and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings.
At that time, Śāriputra, seeing such a marvel, was filled with joy and leaped for gladness, and he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How extraordinary!
World-Honored One!"
"How marvelous! O Sugata!

You have accomplished such great majestic power that you enable us to see the worlds in the direction above, as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Ganges Rivers, where countless bodhisattva-mahāsattvas perform the various distinct practices of the bodhisattva path, and where countless Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas benefit sentient beings through various skillful means."
How extraordinary!
World-Honored One! How rare!

"Sugata! The Buddhas have accomplished the vast and sublime Dharma, which enables Bodhisattvas to resolve their minds and seek that vast and sublime Dharma accomplished by the Buddhas—namely, unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.

The Buddhas have accomplished the vast and sublime Dharma, which enables Bodhisattvas to resolve their minds and seek the vast and sublime Dharma accomplished by the Buddhas—namely, unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
through this, they are able to cultivate the perfections of the provisions and swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes.
Then, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If there are those who wish to attain a superior and unshakable rebirth in the human realm, they should cultivate the distinguished wholesome karma that brings about such a state, as did the Universal Monarch;

if there are those who wish to attain a superior and unshakable rebirth in the celestial realm, they should cultivate the distinguished roots of goodness that bring about such a state, as did Śakra, Lord of the Devas."

If there is one who wishes to sustain their lifespan for a long duration without fluctuation, they should cultivate the sublime meditative absorption capable of inducing that state, such as that of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Thus, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to become the foremost, truly pure field of merit in the world; or to become the greatest Dharma teacher in the trichiliocosm; or likewise to become an unshakable Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, they should resolutely resolve their mind to seek all-knowledge.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.

If one resolutely generates the mind seeking all-knowledge, that person will certainly become the foremost, truly pure field of merit in the world; they will also become the greatest Dharma teacher in the trichiliocosm, and will further become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, bringing benefit, peace, and happiness to all sentient beings.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 582. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part Five of the Eleventh Chapter on the Perfection of Giving. At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"Is it possible for an initial thought to be superior to a subsequent thought?
The World-Honored One replied, "Excellent!"
Excellent! You are able to inquire of the Tathāgata about such a profound meaning.

Listen attentively, and I shall explain it for you. There is indeed the principle that an initial thought may be superior to a subsequent thought; namely, although the various untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*) of Arhats are free from all afflictions within themselves, they cannot yet transform immeasurable sentient beings, causing them all to resolve their minds and abandon all afflictions.

When a Bodhisattva first gives rise to the great mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), although they have not yet severed the afflictions within themselves, they are able to universally transform immeasurable sentient beings, causing them all to resolve their minds and abandon all afflictions; thus, through successive stages, they benefit immeasurable sentient beings.
This is what is meant by the sense that the initial mind is superior to subsequent minds.

Furthermore, there are the various untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*) of Pratyekabuddhas; although they are free from all afflictions within their own bodies, they cannot transform immeasurable sentient beings, causing them all to resolve to abandon their afflictions.

When a Bodhisattva first generates the mind of great enlightenment (*mahābodhicitta*), although they have not yet severed the afflictions within their own body, they are able to universally transform immeasurable sentient beings, causing them all to resolve to abandon their afflictions, and thereby benefiting immeasurable sentient beings in succession. This is the sense in which the initial mind is superior to the subsequent mind.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva’s great mind of enlightenment is practiced, cultivated, or frequently applied, it can fully bring forth the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as well as other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas. By this, one can swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), and through this, transform and deliver immeasurable sentient beings, causing them to attain the fruits of the vehicles of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, or to realize unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, or to cultivate the sublime wholesome karma of humans and devas, thereby attaining the bliss of humans and devas and abandoning the suffering of the evil realms."

Although the untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*) of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cause their own bodies to realize the bliss of nirvāṇa, they cannot induce the perfection of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, nor the other immeasurable and boundless qualities of a Buddha. Furthermore, they cannot attain the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), nor can they transform and deliver immeasurable sentient beings, causing them to attain the fruits of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha vehicles, or to realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), or to cultivate the sublime wholesome karma of humans and devas, thereby attaining the happiness of humans and devas and abandoning the suffering of the evil realms. This is what is meant by the sense that the initial mind is superior to the subsequent mind.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

The power of the great bodhicitta generated by a bodhisattva is exceptionally sublime. If they cultivate it well, they will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. They are able to bestow upon sentient beings unerring predictions, declaring:

'In this very manner, after such a number of kalpas in future ages, these sentient beings shall transmigrate through birth and death while practicing the bodhisattva path, and they shall realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, bringing great benefit to all sentient beings.'"
Or he may prophesy:

"Such and such a sentient being, after passing through so many kalpas in the future world, wandering through birth and death while practicing the path of a pratyekabuddha, shall encounter the right conditions among humans or devas to realize pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, possessing the six supernormal powers and dwelling in sovereign peace and happiness."
Or he may prophesy:

"Such and such a sentient being, after passing through so many kalpas in the future world, wandering through birth and death while practicing the path of a śrāvaka, shall attain the fruit of a śrāvaka among humans and devas."
Or he may prophesy:

"Such and such a sentient being, having performed wholesome or unwholesome karma in a future age, will pass through so many kalpas, taking birth in the realms of humans or devas, or falling into the evil destinies within the cycle of birth and death."
It is not the case that Pratyekabuddhas are able to bestow upon sentient beings unerring predictions; that is to say, they cannot predict for Bodhisattvas, saying:
"In the future, after such a number of kalpas, you shall attain Buddhahood, with such-and-such a name."
Nor can he declare:

"Such a sentient being, after passing through so many kalpas in a future world, will certainly attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, or the fruit of a śrāvaka, or will experience various sufferings and pleasures in the good or evil realms."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, it is not the case that a śrāvaka can bestow a prediction upon another; even those who are able to bestow such predictions have all heard it from the Buddha. This is what is meant by the meaning that the initial resolve is superior to subsequent resolves. "Moreover, Śāriputra!"

Once the Bodhisattva has resolved upon the great mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), desiring to benefit all beings throughout the future, at that time the great earth, the mountains, and the oceans shake and tremble in six ways. The Māra King is struck with terror, while the devas, nāgas, and spirits all rejoice greatly, saying:
"The Bodhisattva shall realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; he will deliver us from the great suffering of birth and death and cause us to attain peace and happiness."

“When Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas abide in their final untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*), such a thing does not occur; this is what is meant by the sense that the initial mind is superior to the subsequent mind.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!”
Even if one were to convert all sentient beings so that they all abide in the fruit of a pratyekabuddha or an arhat, they would not thereby be able to embrace the pāramitās or omniscience;

however, if one instructs and exhorts a bodhisattva to generate the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, one will thereby enable them to embrace the pāramitās of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as well as omniscience.

Why is this? Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot accomplish unsurpassed bodhi because the resolve they have generated is extremely weak and inferior; it is only through bodhisattvas that unsurpassed bodhi can be accomplished. This is the meaning of the initial resolve being superior to subsequent resolves.
"Therefore, those who wish to realize unsurpassed bodhi should all resolve their minds to seek omniscience.
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How should one know the characteristics of the various bodhisattvas?"
"What kind of practice must one cultivate to obtain the name 'Bodhisattva'?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:

"If there is one who can give rise to the mind of great bodhi and diligently practices the pāramitās of generosity, pure morality, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom without weariness of heart; and who, even when encountering various evil friends or conditions for regression, does not yield or retreat—this is the mark of a Bodhisattva. One who possesses these marks is called a Bodhisattva."
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If sentient beings cultivate various wholesome dharmas with a mind free from weariness, uphold pure precepts without ever violating them, and always delight in bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings; if they remain undaunted even when encountering adverse conditions, and according to what they practice and learn, vow to realize awakening together with all sentient beings for ultimate peace and happiness—this is the mark of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. One who possesses these marks is called a bodhisattva.
Then, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How should one understand the profound meaning of what the Buddha has taught—that the mind of a bodhisattva surpasses the untainted minds of all pratyekabuddhas and arhats?”
“We only pray that the World-Honored One will explain this meaning for us, so that we may understand it and uphold it without error!
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:
“Do you think that a bodhisattva’s mind still possesses the afflictions of greed, hatred, delusion, and conceit, as well as other secondary afflictions?”
Śāriputra said: “So it is, World-Honored One!”
"So it is! Well-gone One!
I maintain that the mind of a bodhisattva still possesses greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and all other secondary afflictions."
The Blessed One again addressed Śāriputra, saying:
“Do you consider that the minds of Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats are free from greed, free from hatred, free from delusion, and free from the secondary afflictions such as pride?”
Śāriputra said: “So it is, World-Honored One!”
"So it is! Sugata!
I consider that the minds of Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats are already free from greed, free from hatred, free from delusion, and free from pride and all other secondary afflictions."
The Blessed One again addressed Śāriputra, saying:

"Do you think that Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats, whose outflows are forever exhausted, are at times able to enter the immeasurable states of loving-kindness and compassion, universally taking as their object the infinite and boundless sentient beings with the desire to cause them to attain happiness and be free from all suffering? Would they truly be able to cause those classes of sentient beings to actually attain happiness and be free from suffering?"
Śāriputra said: “No, World-Honored One!”

"No, Sugata! Those Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats lack all skillful means; how could they enter the immeasurables of loving-kindness and compassion, universally taking as their object infinite and boundless sentient beings, and truly cause those beings to attain happiness and be free from suffering?"
One should merely temporarily engage in such contemplation through provisional imagination.

All bodhisattvas who have generated the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) resolutely seek the wisdom of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), desiring to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings until the end of the future, without interruption. Therefore, when a bodhisattva enters the meditative absorption of compassion (*maitrīkaruṇā-samādhi*) with the intent to cause immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to attain peace and happiness and to be freed from all suffering, those who lack heavy obscurations actually attain happiness and are freed from all suffering at that very moment. How much more so when they attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening—could they not then truly cause all classes of sentient beings to attain happiness and be freed from all suffering!
For this reason, it is possible that a Bodhisattva can truly bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings at all times without interruption;

however, it is impossible that if Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats—filling the entire Jambudvīpa and endowed with the eight liberations—were simultaneously to enter the immeasurable concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-apramāṇa-samādhi*) with the desire to cause immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to attain peace and happiness, there would be even one among them who actually attained such happiness.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.

For this reason, the minds of bodhisattvas are the most excellent, the most superior, the most venerable, the most sublime, the most wondrous, the most exquisite, the highest, and the unsurpassed among the untainted minds of all pratyekabuddhas and arhats.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Suppose all sentient beings throughout the ten directions were to exhaust all outflows and become arhats, endowed with various merits such as the six supernormal powers and the eight liberations; and suppose each of them were to magically transform themselves into ten billion demonic armies—would these demonic armies be numerous?
Śāriputra said: “Very many,
World-Honored One!”
"Very many, Sugata!
The number of Arhats alone is already vast; how much more so when each one of them can further manifest ten billion demonic armies!"
"Could the measure of these demonic armies ever be known?
The World-Honored One again addressed Śāriputra, saying:

"Suppose there were as many immeasurable and innumerable demonic armies as there are Arhats who have been thus transformed; would they have the power to cause the mind of even a single non-regressive Bodhisattva to change, even for a moment?"
Śāriputra said: “No, World-Honored One!”
"No, Sugata! Even such immeasurable and innumerable hosts of Māras cannot cause the mind of a single non-regressive Bodhisattva to undergo any change."
The World-Honored One again addressed Śāriputra, saying: "What do you think?
Between the mind of an Arhat who has thus forever exhausted all outflows and the mind of a non-retrogressive Bodhisattva, which possesses the greater power and majesty?"
Śāriputra said: “As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, the mental power of a non-regressive bodhisattva is superior, and not that of an incalculable number of arhats.”
The Buddha said: "So it is! It is just as you have said."

You should now observe that these immeasurable Arhats—whose minds are free from outflows and eternally devoid of greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and the like—each can further manifest ten billion valiant māra armies. Yet, even if all these māra armies exhaust their supernatural powers, they cannot cause the mind of a single Bodhisattva who possesses greed, hatred, delusion, or pride to undergo any change.
From this, one should know that the power of a bodhisattva’s mind surpasses the minds of arhats who have exhausted all outflows. Furthermore,
Śāriputra, what do you think?

Who is the most eminent, the most excellent, the most venerable, the highest, the most sublime, the most subtle, the supreme, and the unsurpassed among those who possess such an arhat’s mind that is free from the afflictions of greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and so forth?

Śāriputra said: "The minds of non-retrogressive bodhisattvas, although they possess afflictions such as greed, hatred, delusion, and pride, are the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the most exalted, the most sublime, the most wondrous, the highest, and the unsurpassed among all untainted arhat-minds."

Why is this? Because even if all the untainted, immeasurable, and boundless minds of Arhats and their emanations were to exhaust their supernatural powers, they could not cause a single bodhisattva who possesses greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and other afflictions to retreat from or alter the bodhicitta.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"I shall now question you; answer as you see fit. What do you think?"
If there were a heap of kacha mani jewels, and among them were placed a single vaidūrya gem, could the radiance and value of the kacha mani jewels possibly outshine that of the vaidūrya?
Śāriputra said: “No, World-Honored One!”
"No, Sugata! The brilliance and value of a single piece of vaidūrya can universally outshine an entire heap of mahākañcana."
Why is this? The vaidūrya jewel is luminous and pure both inside and out, whereas the kācamaṇi is not so;
the vaidūrya jewel possesses a lustrous and moist radiance, whereas the kācamaṇi does not.
The natural color of vaidūrya gem is deep blue, whereas the kācamaṇi is not so;
the lineage of the vaidūrya gem is superior, whereas the kācamaṇi is not so;
the majestic power of the vaidūrya gem is vast and great, whereas the kācamaṇi is not so.
The precious vaidūrya gem is of immeasurable value, whereas the kaccamanī is not so;

the vaidūrya gem arises from the oceanic islands through the sovereign power of the karma of noble beings, while the kaccamanī, whether of high or low quality, is produced by human craftsmanship for common use.
"Therefore, the brilliance and value of vaidūrya outshine all karketana mani jewels.
At that time, the World-Honored One told Śāriputra:

"The mind of a non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this; it is universally able to outshine the minds of all pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas, just as vaidūrya outshines a heap of karketanas."
Observing this principle, I speak thus:

the non-retrogressive mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the most sublime, the most wondrous, the most exquisite, the highest, and the unsurpassed among the untainted minds of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas that are forever free from afflictions.
The mind of compassion conjoined with loving-kindness belonging to non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas can enable sentient beings to attain happiness and be free from suffering;
whereas the mind of compassion conjoined with loving-kindness belonging to Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas consists merely of conceptual imagination and lacks practical efficacy.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

There are Arhats who have forever exhausted all outflows and possess various merits such as the six supernormal powers and the eight liberations; they may use their supernatural power to hurl this world and place it in another direction, yet they cannot cause the mind of a non-retrogressive Bodhisattva to undergo any change."

Furthermore, Śāriputra, there are Arhats who have forever exhausted all outflows and possess various meritorious qualities such as the six supernormal powers and the eight liberations; they may, by means of their spiritual power, dry up the waters of the great ocean, yet they cannot cause the mind of a non-retrogressive Bodhisattva to undergo any change.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

There are Arhats who have forever exhausted all outflows and possess various meritorious qualities such as the six supernormal powers and the eight liberations; they may, by means of their supernatural power, blow apart worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, reducing all the Kings of Mountains, Sumerus, therein to mere ash and dust, yet they cannot cause the mind of a non-regressive Bodhisattva to undergo any transformation.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, there are Arhats who have forever exhausted all outflows and possess various meritorious qualities such as the six supernormal powers and the eight liberations. By means of their supernormal power, they can blow away worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, causing even the fierce, blazing flames of the great kalpa-fire to be instantly extinguished; yet they cannot cause the mind of a non-retrogressive Bodhisattva to undergo any change.
For this reason, I say:

the non-retrogressive mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the most sublime, the most wondrous, the most exquisite, the highest, and the unsurpassed among the untainted minds of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas that are forever free from afflictions.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How extraordinary!
World-Honored One!”
"How marvelous!
Well-gone One!
The mind of a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with such great majestic power that śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot alter it."
At that time, the Buddha said to Śāriputra: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said. Why is this? Śāriputra!
The words of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are non-dual; the meanings spoken by the Buddhas are all true and not false. You should uphold them and extensively explain them to others.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

The sentient beings of the worlds in the ten directions are immeasurable and boundless. Suppose that within each of the worlds in the ten directions—as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River—one were to transform every single grain of sand into as many sentient beings as there are grains;

or suppose that the earth, water, fire, and air of immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless worlds in the ten directions were all crushed into atoms, and each atom were transformed into as many sentient beings as there are atoms. Would these sentient beings be many?
Śāriputra said, “Very many,
World-Honored One!”
"Very many, Sugata! the Buddha said.

"Suppose all these sentient beings were simultaneously to become arhats, forever exhausting all outflows, possessing various merits such as the six supernormal powers and the eight liberations, and achieving vast and sovereign supernatural faculties, such that every one of them was exactly like Mahāgovinda."

Suppose each and every one of these great arhats were able to manifest as many evil Māras, and each of those evil Māras were further able to manifest as many brave and powerful elephant troops, cavalry, chariot troops, and infantry; could the number of such armies be known?
Śāriputra said: “No, World-Honored One!”
"No, Sugata! The Buddha said:

"Suppose there were a son or daughter of good family who could count as many worlds as there are in a trichiliocosm, and who, by means of supernormal powers, could shatter all the armies of Māra and cause them to retreat and disperse."
"What do you think?
Is the supernatural power and majesty of this son or daughter of good family vast and great? Śāriputra replied:
“Vast, World-Honored One! Vast!”
“Sugata! The supernatural power and majesty of this son or daughter of good family are invincible and inconceivable.
The Buddha said:

"Even if the men and women described above were as numerous as all sentient beings previously mentioned, and if each of these men and women were to remain for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges within the infinite, countless, and boundless worlds of the ten directions, and if in every thought-moment they were to manifest as many evil Māras as previously described, and each of those evil Māras were again to manifest as many brave and powerful armies of elephants and horses as previously described—even so, they could not cause the Bodhisattva’s mind of non-retrogression to undergo any change."
Furthermore, Śāriputra, what do you think? Suppose all those sentient beings were to become Arhats,

and each one were to manifest as many Māras as there are [sentient beings], and each of those Māras possessed great supernormal powers— comparing such supernormal powers with the supernormal power inherent in the mind of a single non-retrogressive Bodhisattva, which would be superior?
Śāriputra said: "The supernormal power possessed by the minds of non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is superior to that. Why is this so? Because—"
"The spiritual powers possessed by the minds of non-retrogressive Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are immeasurable, innumerable, inconceivable, and inexpressible.
The World-Honored One further addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"What do you think?"

Compared to the supernormal powers possessed by the Arhats who have attained immeasurable and boundless great supernormal faculties as previously described, who could say that the supernormal powers belonging to the mind of a non-retrogressive Bodhisattva Mahāsattva are the most excellent, the most superior, the most noble, the most high, the most wondrous, the most subtle, the most supreme, or the unsurpassed?

Śāriputra said: "As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is able to describe the supernormal powers possessed by the minds of those non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; compared to all the supernormal powers possessed by the aforementioned immeasurable and boundless arhats of great supernatural power, [the powers of the bodhisattvas] are the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the most sublime, the most wondrous, the most exquisite, the highest, and the unsurpassed."

Why is this so? Because there is no power possessed by the minds of non-retrogressive Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas that can equal the power of their minds associated with all-knowledge (sarvajñatā), except for that very mind itself.

By virtue of these causes and conditions, the supernormal powers possessed by the minds of non-regressive Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas can be known only by a Buddha and spoken of only by a Buddha; among all other supernormal powers, they are the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the most exalted, the most wondrous, the most subtle, the highest, and the unsurpassed.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said. Why is this? Śāriputra!

The mind of a non-regressing bodhisattva mahāsattva cannot be altered by any other sentient being; nor is there anyone who truly knows it or can describe it, except for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, who alone knows that bodhisattva’s irreversible mind and proclaims it to all sentient beings exactly as it is.
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked Śāriputra:
"By what causes and conditions is the mind of a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva unchangeable?"
Śāriputra said: "When Bodhisattvas practice generosity, there is none that does not take omniscience as its object; their minds are firm and cannot be shaken."
When one thus attains the stage of non-retrogression, the mind does not undergo transformation in accordance with conditions.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
It is as if there were a person skilled in adjudicating legal cases, who had repeatedly settled disputes among countless assemblies of elders, householders, and merchants."

Because he was impoverished, he frequently borrowed goods and wealth from elders, householders, and others; fearing that they might come to demand repayment and that he would lack the means to pay them back, he consequently sought refuge with the king, hoping to avoid imprisonment.
At that time, because the creditors were terrified of the king, they did not dare to seize, drag, or humiliate that man.
Why was this? Because the power of the king upon whom he relied was so great as to be difficult to withstand.

Thus, whether it be a bodhisattva who has first resolved for awakening or one who is irreversible, all possess great spiritual power by virtue of relying upon the knowledge of all modes; neither any pratyekabuddha nor any arhat can cause their minds to waver.
Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Just as a person who relies upon a king, though extremely poor and destitute, is not subjected to humiliation;

so too, a bodhisattva who relies upon the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) cannot be shaken by those of the two vehicles or by Māras, but can instead subdue all Māras. Compared to those of the two vehicles, he is the most eminent, the most superior, the most honored, the most exalted, the most wonderful, the most subtle, the highest, and the unsurpassed.

Therefore, a bodhisattva who wishes not to fall back should always rely upon the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) to cultivate the bodhisattva practice, and should not take pleasure in other vehicles.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked:
“What kind of bodhisattva is surpassed by pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas?”
Śāriputra said: "If bodhisattvas, upon hearing an exposition of the superior qualities of pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas, feel admiration in their hearts and think:
'How may I attain such dharmas?'"

Furthermore, they take deep delight in and become attached to the teachings of the two vehicles; because these bodhisattvas give rise to such improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*), they are overcome by all pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas.
Then, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked the venerable Śāriputra:
"For what reason do you say that this mental engagement of a bodhisattva is called 'unreasonable'? Śāriputra replied:

"Because this obstructs the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) and causes the mind that can bring forth the knowledge of all modes to gradually diminish and recede, it is called the bodhisattva’s improper mental attention (ayoniśomanasikāra)."

For example, when a practitioner of yoga seeks to realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and joyfully aspires to enter the state of rightness and transcendence (samyaktva-niyāma), if greed, hatred, or delusion should arise due to conditions, they would prevent the arousal of the mind of an arhat; because these states create obstructions and hindrances that cause [the realization] to gradually diminish and recede, they are therefore called "unwise attention" (ayoniśo-manasikāra).

In this way, when a bodhisattva seeks great enlightenment, if they give rise to mental attention associated with the two vehicles, it obstructs omniscience and diminishes the bodhicitta; therefore, this is called irrational mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*).
"If bodhisattvas possess such mental engagement, they will be overcome by those of the two vehicles.
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:

"If bodhisattvas give rise to a mental engagement associated with the two vehicles, they will be overcome by those of the two vehicles; one should know that they do not enter the ranks of the bodhisattvas."
Why is this? Śāriputra!

A bodhisattva seeks only unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; if they give rise to mental orientations associated with the two vehicles, they contravene their original aspiration and will be unable to realize all-knowledge.

Just as when the afflictions manifest in a stream-enterer (srotāpanna), they contradict what is sought—namely, either knowledge or abandonment—and because they diligently seek such knowledge and abandonment, they are called "stream-enterers. It is not that the manifestation of afflictions possesses the sense of diligent seeking.
Why is this? Śāriputra,
one who has entered the stream seeks two types of thorough knowledge:
There are two types of thorough knowledge: first, thorough knowledge by wisdom (*jñāna-parijñā*), and second, thorough knowledge by abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*).

Since both the active manifestation of afflictions (*kleśa*) and the two types of seeking (*pariṣkāra-paryeṣaṇā*) are destroyed [by these], a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) should always diligently strive for thorough knowledge by wisdom in order to extinguish all afflictions.
In this way, if a bodhisattva gives rise to mental attention associated with the two vehicles, they contravene the omniscience that is the primary object of their aspiration.
If bodhisattvas distance themselves from the mind and mental factors that aspire for omniscience, they cannot be called true bodhisattvas.
Why is this? Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva must always aspire for the mind of omniscience (sarvajñajñāna) without interruption.
If bodhisattvas abide in the bodhisattva-mind, neither those of the two vehicles nor Māras can overcome them; rather, they are able to overcome those of the two vehicles and the Māras.

Just as a skilled archer, remaining in his place of training, cannot be overcome by any enemy but is able to subdue enemies and remain free from all fear, so too the bodhisattva abiding in the bodhisattva-mind cannot be destroyed by any adverse conditions, yet is able to destroy all the activities of the Māras.
If they hear the teaching of the Dharma of the Two Vehicles being proclaimed, they immediately form this thought:
"I shall realize unexcelled bodhi, and for the sake of all sentient beings, I shall also proclaim such a teaching of the Dharma."

Now, the World-Honored One, the Able Quiescent One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, proclaims the teachings corresponding to the two vehicles for those individuals belonging to the lineages of pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas.
"When I attain Buddhahood in a future age, I shall likewise preach such teachings for these classes of sentient beings to enable them to obtain benefit and happiness.

Thus, a bodhisattva who dwells with skillful means within the bodhisattva mind is not harmed even upon hearing teachings associated with the two vehicles; that is to say, although they hear those associated teachings, they feel no attachment or defilement toward the two vehicles.
In this way, when a bodhisattva abides in the bodhisattva-mind, they cannot be overcome by the two vehicles or by Māra; rather, they are able to overcome the two vehicles and Māra.
This is just as a practitioner of yoga, having attained skillfulness in both the object and meditative concentration, cannot be overcome.
Why is this? Because the mind, having become fixed upon its object and being well-cultivated and purified, has attained mastery.
Thus, when a bodhisattva abides in the bodhisattva-mind, neither those of the two vehicles nor evil Māras can overcome or subdue them.
"Why is this? It is because these bodhisattvas are never separated from the mind of a bodhisattva.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:
“Are all bodhisattvas— whether they have first resolved their minds toward awakening, whether they have already attained non-retrogression, or whether they are seated upon the seat of enlightenment—

inconquerable? Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra replied, “One should know that all bodhisattvas— whether they have first resolved their minds toward awakening, whether they have already attained non-retrogression, or whether they are seated upon the seat of enlightenment— are indeed inconquerable.”

Why is this? Śāriputra, it is because no adverse conditions whatsoever can cause these bodhisattvas to abandon their original vows. That is to say, when bodhisattvas resolve upon bodhicitta and desire to constantly benefit all sentient beings, these two matters—their vow and their resolve—are so firm that no adverse conditions can shake them. If bodhisattvas abide in this mind, neither those of the two vehicles nor Māras can overcome or subdue them.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Whether Tathāgatas have first attained Buddhahood or have already attained Buddhahood and remained for hundreds of thousands of years, they all do not abandon the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*), and at all times they realize omniscience.

In this way, whether a bodhisattva has first resolved their mind, has attained non-retrogression, or is seated upon the seat of enlightenment, they never for a moment abandon the mental attention that seeks to realize all-knowledge by taking it as their object at all times.
Śāriputra said: “If this is so, what distinctions are there among the various stages of a bodhisattva?
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra replied:
"The mental states of Bodhisattvas at all stages are without distinction; there is only a difference in the speed with which they attain Buddhahood.
That is to say, throughout the initial, middle, and final stages of a Bodhisattva’s mind, they always seek to bring forth unsurpassed enlightenment, abiding in this mind without ever regressing."
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Just as an arhat never regresses from the state of an arhat—that is, the untainted mind (anāsrava-citta) is necessarily without regression—a bodhisattva is likewise;
they never regress from the mind of great enlightenment (mahābodhicitta).
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, what do you think?
If an arhat’s mind were subject to regression, would he be a true arhat?"
Śāriputra said: “No, Venerable One!”
"If an Arhat’s mind should undergo regression, you should know that he is one of overweening pride (adhimāna) and has certainly not attained the fruit of Arhatship.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:

"It is the same for Bodhisattvas; if there is a Bodhisattva who regresses from the bodhicitta, you should know that he previously claimed to be a Bodhisattva but is not a true Bodhisattva. He is one of overweening pride who defiles the assembly of Bodhisattvas, just as a foul snail defiles clear water so that it is unfit for drinking."
Śāriputra said: “So it is! So it is!”

You should know that such individuals, their minds obscured by ignorance, claim for themselves the title of Bodhisattva; yet they have not actually entered the ranks of true Bodhisattvas and possess nothing but an empty name.

For example, it is like a man who has fully developed male organs, while another with defective organs claims to be a man; the latter has only empty words and lacks the actual substance. So it is with these Bodhisattvas: having regressed from the bodhicitta, they possess only an empty name and are not true Bodhisattvas.
Just as one who lacks sense organs is called a paṇḍaka, one who has regressed from the bodhicitta is called a counterfeit bodhisattva.

Therefore, throughout the initial, middle, and final stages, a bodhisattva must remain resolutely non-regressive regarding the great bodhicitta; if one regresses from this mind, they are no longer a bodhisattva.
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked Śāriputra:
"If bodhisattvas wish to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, what kind of corresponding mental attention (*manasikāra*) should they arouse?"

Śāriputra said: "If bodhisattvas wish to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, they should correctly arouse the mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all modes; all bodhisattva dharmas should be established within such mental engagement."
If bodhisattvas dwell in this mental engagement and practice generosity, these bodhisattvas are then able to dedicate it toward omniscience.
If bodhisattvas thus dedicate it toward omniscience, these bodhisattvas embrace the perfection of generosity;
if bodhisattvas cannot dedicate it toward omniscience, the generosity practiced by those bodhisattvas is not called the perfection of generosity.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
When bodhisattvas practice giving, they may think:

'I am relinquishing this small portion, not relinquishing that small portion; I am giving this object, not giving that object; I am giving to such a class of beings, not giving to such a class of beings.'"

Because these bodhisattvas are hindered from omniscience by such reflections, they must pass a long time before they can attain it; it is only after a vast duration that their perfection of the pāramitā of generosity becomes fully accomplished.

Therefore, a bodhisattva who wishes to be unimpeded in the knowledge of all-knowledge, who wishes to swiftly realize the knowledge of all-knowledge, and who wishes to swiftly bring the perfection of generosity to completion, should abandon such discriminative thoughts; they should relinquish all portions, give away all things, and practice equal giving toward all classes of beings.
Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
If bodhisattvas wish to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should abide in the perfection of generosity; they should abide in the perfection of generosity in this manner.

"If a bodhisattva, during the first part of the day, were able to provide various kinds of excellent food and drink as offerings to sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; having made these offerings, further bestow upon them exquisite garments of golden hue;

and during the middle part of the day, likewise provide various kinds of excellent food and drink as offerings to sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; having made these offerings, further bestow upon them exquisite garments of golden hue;

and during the latter part of the day, likewise provide various kinds of excellent food and drink as offerings to sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; having made these offerings, further bestow upon them exquisite garments of golden hue;"
It is likewise during the three watches of the night.

If such giving continues without interruption for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, yet these bodhisattvas do not dedicate the merit toward the attainment of the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), it is called "giving" but not the "perfection of giving" (*dānapāramitā*);
only if they can dedicate it toward the attainment of the knowledge of all-knowledge is it called the "perfection of giving."
This means that when practicing generosity, one does not set limits; rather, whether the amount is great or small, one generates a vast mind and gives everything universally to all sentient beings.
"In this way, when a bodhisattva practices generosity, although they do not discard much but give everything, they thereby fulfill the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā)."

Why is this? It is because one practices the perfection of generosity with the desire to realize immeasurable Buddha-dharmas; if, at the time of giving, the mind is limited, one will certainly be unable to realize immeasurable Buddha-dharmas.

If bodhisattvas practice giving with a limited mind, those bodhisattvas will certainly be unable to realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), and they will certainly be unable to fulfill the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā). Therefore, bodhisattvas who wish to realize the immeasurable knowledge of all modes should give rise to an immeasurable mind and practice giving.

If bodhisattvas practice generosity with a limited mind, these bodhisattvas embrace stinginess and are unable to relinquish it forever; they cannot embrace the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*). Conversely, by being the opposite of this, they are able to realize the knowledge of all modes and bring the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) to fulfillment.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
When bodhisattvas wish to practice giving, they should give rise to this thought:
'I shall practice immeasurable giving; until I have realized unsurpassed bodhi, I shall first practice the gift of material wealth toward all sentient beings.'"
"If I realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I shall practice the gift of Dharma for all sentient beings.

This means that as long as one has not realized unsurpassed enlightenment, one should first gather in sentient beings through material gifts, causing them to leave behind the suffering of poverty and attain worldly happiness;

once one has realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, one should gather in sentient beings through the gift of Dharma, causing them to leave behind afflictions and attain supramundane bliss.
Just as when a person serves a king, they first obtain food and clothing to support their wife and children, and later, by winning the king’s favor, they acquire great wealth;

thus both themselves and their family enjoy prosperity, security, and happiness—so too does a bodhisattva, seeking to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, perform hundreds of thousands of difficult and painful practices. First, through the gift of material wealth, they gather in sentient beings and cause them to leave behind the various sufferings of worldly poverty; subsequently, upon realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, they instruct and guide all classes of sentient beings with the untainted Dharma, causing them to be liberated from the manifold sufferings of birth and death.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

Suppose hundreds of thousands of sentient beings serve a prince, exerting themselves day and night; at that time, the prince provides them with clothing, food and drink, bedding, and other necessities according to their merit. Later, when he ascends the throne, he rewards them with rank and emoluments commensurate with their former diligence and the weight of the responsibilities they were capable of bearing—whether as overseers of enterprises, or of rivers and plains, or of great cities, or of border passes, or of villages and towns, or of military affairs."

In this way, when a bodhisattva seeks omniscience, prior to realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they first gather sentient beings through material wealth; subsequently, upon realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they provide instruction and guidance with the unsurpassed Dharma according to the varying levels of wisdom of those sentient beings, causing them to abide in the fruit of arhatship, or the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of stream-entry, or in the ten paths of wholesome action, or in the sublime state of a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

These bodhisattvas, seeking great enlightenment and practicing the bodhisattva path, bring about great benefit for all sentient beings even before they have realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening;
and when they do realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, they likewise bring about great benefit for sentient beings."
Even after his parinirvāṇa, he will likewise bring great benefit to immeasurable and boundless sentient beings.
It is just as when a prince has not yet succeeded to the throne, he brings great benefit to all sentient beings;
and once he has succeeded to the throne, he also brings great benefit to sentient beings.
Even after his life has ended, he will likewise bring great benefit to sentient beings.
Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra,
it is like a person who serves a king with such diligent application over a long period of time that, as time passes, his rank and emoluments gradually increase.
In this way, as a bodhisattva seeks all-knowledge and applies themselves with such diligence over a long period of time, their merits gradually increase accordingly.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

Before these bodhisattvas have realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, they gather in sentient beings through material gifts—namely, by means of various garments, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other resources—skillfully employing expedient means to gather them in and benefit them.

When one realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, one gathers in and benefits all sentient beings through the Dharma; that is, by means of the various perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as well as other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas; or by means of the various applications of mindfulness, right efforts, bases of power, faculties, powers, factors of awakening, and factors of the path, as well as other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas; or by means of the various meritorious actions of giving, the meritorious actions of ethical discipline, the meritorious actions of cultivation, and other immeasurable mundane wholesome dharmas.

Even after his parinirvāṇa, he likewise brings great benefit to immeasurable and boundless sentient beings; that is to say, by making offerings to the Buddha’s *śarīra*, or by upholding, reciting, and practicing according to the instructions of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed True Dharma, all shall obtain boundless and vast benefits—namely, the happiness of humans and devas, or parinirvāṇa, or the ultimate peace and bliss of Great Bodhi.
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said to Śāriputra: "So it is! So it is!"
It is exactly as you have said.

What you, O Venerable One, have spoken is entirely in accordance with the truth; therefore, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has always declared that among the assembly of śrāvakas, you are foremost in wisdom and eloquence.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

For example, genuine gold constantly brings great benefit to sentient beings: whether it is still within the ore, when it has been extracted from the ore, when it has been transformed into various ornaments, or when it is sold and used to purchase other goods—it always brings great benefit to immeasurable and boundless sentient beings according to their respective needs."

In this way, while a bodhisattva practices the bodhisattva conduct and has not yet realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, they bring great benefit to all sentient beings; that is to say, through skillful means, they gather in and benefit them according to their needs by means of both material wealth and the Dharma.

When one realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, one turns the sublime wheel of Dharma to bring great benefit; that is to say, one proclaims that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is neither permanent nor impermanent, as it is unapprehendable; one proclaims that the aggregates of feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are likewise neither permanent nor impermanent, as they too are unapprehendable.

One proclaims that the sense base of the eye (*cakṣur-āyatana*) is neither permanent nor impermanent, as it is unapprehendable; one proclaims that the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are likewise neither permanent nor impermanent, as they too are unapprehendable.

One proclaims that the sense base of forms (*rūpa-āyatana*) is neither permanent nor impermanent, as it is unapprehendable; one proclaims that the sense bases of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena (*dharma-āyatana*) are likewise neither permanent nor impermanent, as they too are unapprehendable.

He teaches that the eye-element’s permanence, impermanence, and so forth are unapprehendable; he teaches that the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-elements’ permanence, impermanence, and so forth are likewise unapprehendable.

He teaches that the form-element’s permanence, impermanence, and so forth are unapprehendable; he teaches that the sound-, odor-, taste-, tangible-, and phenomena-elements’ permanence, impermanence, and so forth are likewise unapprehendable.

He teaches that the eye-consciousness-element’s permanence, impermanence, and so forth are unapprehendable; he teaches that the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness-elements’ permanence, impermanence, and so forth are likewise unapprehendable.

He teaches that the eye-contact’s being permanent or impermanent is unapprehendable; he teaches that the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact’s being permanent or impermanent is likewise unapprehendable.

He teaches that the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, whether permanent or impermanent, are unapprehendable; he teaches that the various feelings produced with the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact as conditions, whether permanent or impermanent, are likewise unapprehendable.

He teaches that the earth element’s being permanent or impermanent is unapprehendable; he teaches that the water-, fire-, wind-, space-, and consciousness-element’s being permanent or impermanent is likewise unapprehendable.

It is taught that causes and conditions, whether permanent or impermanent, are unapprehendable; it is taught that the immediately preceding condition, the object condition, and the dominant condition, whether permanent or impermanent, are likewise unapprehendable.

It is taught that ignorance, whether permanent or impermanent, is unapprehendable; it is taught that volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age and death, whether permanent or impermanent, are likewise unapprehendable.

It is taught that a self, whether permanent or impermanent, is unapprehendable; it is taught that a sentient being, a life-principle, a living being, a nourisher, a person, an individual, a mind-born, a youth, an agent, an experiencer, a knower, or a seer, whether permanent or impermanent, are likewise unapprehendable.

He proclaims that in the desire realm, permanence, impermanence, and so forth are unapprehendable; he likewise proclaims that in the form and formless realms, permanence, impermanence, and so forth are also unapprehendable.
Thus, by proclaiming various Dharma gates, he brings great benefit to all sentient beings.
After his parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma, the Semblance Dharma, and the śarīra relics will bring great benefit to all sentient beings;
the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not possess such qualities.
Therefore, when the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cultivates the bodhisattva practices, they constantly bring great benefit to sentient beings.

For this reason, it is said that among those of the two vehicles, the assembly of bodhisattvas is the most eminent, the most excellent, the most honored, the most sublime, the most wondrous, the most exquisite, the highest, and the unsurpassed.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Ānanda, saying:
“You should receive and uphold what the Śāriputras and others have said:

‘The assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, donning the armor of great vows and proceeding toward great enlightenment, endowed with supreme skillful means and superior intention, practices the perfection of giving, relinquishing both Dharma and wealth without defilement or attachment.’”

When the Blessed One had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Śāriputra, the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, the Venerable Ānanda, along with the other śrāvakas, the assembly of bodhisattvas, and the rest of the great multitude—including gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly delighted; they believed, accepted, and practiced it.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle Five Hundred and Eighty-Three.
